Zion Draws The Crowds—These 3 Nearby Parks Are Where to Escape Them

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1086 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that just beyond Zion lie some truly incredible desert landscapes to wander without the crowds.
  • According to recent reports, entry queues and crowded trails come with the territory at bucket-list national parks like Zion.
  • According to recent reports, but I’ll be honest: On my recent trip to Zion, the trails felt more like a conga line than a wilderness escape.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that just beyond Zion lie some truly incredible desert landscapes to wander without the crowds. (Photo: Arrterra via Getty).

According to recent reports, entry queues and crowded trails come with the territory at bucket-list national parks like Zion. With nearly 5 million visitors in 2025, it ranked as the second-most visited national park in the U.S. Once you make it through the entry gate, though, the payoff is real. Visitors walk beneath towering Navajo sandstone cliffs and wade the Virgin River deep into The Narrows. If luck’s on your side, you might even win the permit lottery to hike to Angels Landing.

According to recent reports, but I’ll be honest: On my recent trip to Zion, the trails felt more like a conga line than a wilderness escape. I was more paranoid than peaceful, constantly stepping aside and watching my footing as I squeezed past other hikers. The incredible beauty of the park draws equally incredible crowds.

The good news is you don’t have to fight for elbow room to soak in Zion’s beauty. Its neighboring state parks, wildernesses, and national forests get a fraction of the attention, but are just as jaw-dropping. Explore the surrounding Greater Zion region, and you’ll unlock hikes through red rock without the gridlock.

Head beyond Zion for these underrated hiking spots instead.

Sources indicate that distance from Zion: 1 hour (West) Entrance fee: $15 per vehicle Best for: Hikers seeking desert variety without a grueling trek. Petrified dunes, sandstone cliffs, slot canyons, and hikeable lava tubes, all in one park.

If Snow Canyon State Park were a DJ, it’d spin a killer geological mashup of 180-million-year-old petrified dunes, Jurassic-period sandstone escarpments, and ancient river-carved slot canyons. The drop: cavernous, jet-black lava tubes you can hike into (headlamp recommended). The park packs a huge punch of diverse terrain you rarely see all in one place. It’s especially family-friendly and a good fit for more casual hikers who want photo-worthy views without a grueling trek.

Sources indicate that catch the park’s greatest hits in one go by linking up the Butterfly Trail, Lava Flow Overlook, West Canyon Overlook, and the Petrified Dunes Loop. The roughly 3-mile loop connects the park’s most notable features. Hikers will see ancient lava flows, winding slickrock passages, and sweeping views down into West Canyon. The petrified dunes along the route steal the show. Hikers walk over rolling hills frozen in time while swirling stripes of orange, cream, and crimson dance underfoot.

Looking for more technical hiking? Tackle the trek to Deidre Peak. The 7.4-mile out-and-back climbs nearly 1,500 feet in elevation and requires a Class 3-4 scramble over rugged sandstone outcrops. The trail crosses into the larger Red Cliffs Desert Reserve, a conservation area protected as a sanctuary for the native Mojave desert tortoise.

Distance from Zion: 1 hour (West) Entrance fee: $5 per vehicle Best for: Hikers and BLM land lovers seeking seclusion and solitude.

In a recent development, beyond Snow Canyon sprawls Red Cliffs National Conservation Area. The nearly 45,000 acres of BLM land sits within the larger Red Cliffs Desert Reserve at the crossroads of the Mojave Desert, Great Basin, and Colorado Plateau. Here you’ll find a mix of plants and wildlife from all three regions. There are two endangered wildflowers that grow only in this corner of Utah: the dwarf bear poppy and Shivwits milkvetch. Both bloom in spring, with peak overlap in late April and early May. Then there’s southern Utah’s classic red sandstone stretching as far as the eye can see.

Popular out-and-back hikes like the 3.5-mile Elephant Arch Trail and 1.6-mile Red Reef Trail show how water and wind erosion turn sandstone landscapes into works of art. Elephant Arch earned its name from a distinct sandstone outcropping that looks uncannily like a trunk, head, and ears. Along the Red Reef Trail, hikers skirt massive, smooth sandstone bowls. These turn into swimming holes during spring rain and monsoon season, which runds July through September.

It has been revealed that the 5-mile Black Gulch and Yellow Knolls Loop drops through a boulder-strewn gulch of dark volcanic rock, then rolls over yellow sandstone knolls. Hikers can also link the Red Reef and Prospector Trails to create a 10.5-mile loop requiring some scrambling and route-finding through remote backcountry canyons. On the return leg, wide views open up to the Pine Valley Mountains in the north, often capped with snow in winter and early spring.

Distance from Zion: 1 hour 15 minutes (Northeast) Entrance fee: None Best for: Hikers looking for trail variety that showcases Utah’s finest terrain.

Recent findings suggest that the state’s largest national forest reveals off a completely different side of southern Utah. Dixie National Forest sprawls across nearly 2 million acres, rising from the desert valley around St. George to peaks above 11,000 feet. Sagebrush, pinyon, and juniper give way to aspen groves and conifer forests as you climb. The higher and farther you hike, the more surprises you’ll find: trout-filled mountain lakes, towering hoodoo spires, and the chance to spot Utah prairie dogs in the wild.

Dixie gives hikers a taste of the same pink-and-orange Claron limestone that made Bryce Canyon famous. The difference? Here, thick stands of ponderosa pine grow right up against the hoodoos. Plus, the trails see a fraction of the foot traffic, so you’ll have the views practically to yourself.

If you want more hoodoo action, check out Thunder Mountain Trail. It winds through what feels like a bite-sized Bryce Canyon. The out-and-back trail climbs more than 1,700 feet over 8.6 miles. You’re rewarded with an unforgettable trek through a maze of spires. For an even more awe-inspiring experience, hike early or late in the day, when low sun turns the Claron limestone a vibrant orange.

Looking for a more Zion-esque experience? Ashdown Gorge Trail echoes the Narrows, minus the permits, rental gear, and crowds. It travels 10 miles from the alpine rim of Cedar Breaks to a creek-carved canyon where red rock walls close in overhead. Heads up: There are two popular ways to hike Ashdown Gorge. You can do an out-and-back that starts at the bottom and heads up into the narrows (recommended), or a point-to-point that requires a shuttle.

Sources indicate that for a longer, relatively flat dayhike, opt for the 11-mile Navajo Lake Loop. The trail circles its namesake, peeking in and out of dense pine, fir, and aspen forest, with shoreline views that make it easy to forget you’re in a red rock wonderland.

#90653. The Glacier Died—And the Trail Runners Started Coming

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2705 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Trailrunnermag ↗ Open Full Page

The Glacier Died—And the Trail Runners Started Coming

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2705 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that I’m standing with Samuel Mendoza on top of Chacaltaya Mountain, 17,785 feet above sea level.
  • Recent findings suggest that directly ahead, the Altiplano—the high plain—stretches from the foot of the mountain.
  • Behind us rises the Huayna Potosí massif.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that I’m standing with Samuel Mendoza on top of Chacaltaya Mountain, 17,785 feet above sea level. Under our feet is a sharp slope of scree, a jumbled descent of rocks with patches of snow. The air is thin, and the vast Bolivian landscape surrounds us.

Recent findings suggest that directly ahead, the Altiplano—the high plain—stretches from the foot of the mountain. El Alto, the chaotic concrete and red brick city that has grown to roughly 900,000 people, lies at the far edge of the plain at 13,000 feet of elevation, crammed against a canyon’s edge. About 1,500 feet below and connected by a series of cable cars, La Paz, Bolivia’s seat of government, sprawls.

Behind us rises the Huayna Potosí massif. The nearly 20,000-foot summit towers above, its glaciated peak passing in and out of fast-moving clouds. About 45 miles to the northwest, Lake Titicaca—the central motif to Inca creation stories—shimmers on the horizon.

It’s here, on this high mountain of almost-bare rock cradled in the Andes, that Mendoza learned to ski.

Located roughly 20 miles north of La Paz, Chacaltaya was once the world’s highest-altitude ski resort. It began in the 1930s when Raúl Posnansky, an engineer and ski enthusiast, recognized the mountain’s potential, according to 2023 reporting by “Radio Ambulante.” Chacaltaya’s glacier, though relatively small in area at roughly 55 acres, was a solid tongue of ice descending the slope. Temperatures up high stayed low, and snow fell heavily and often during the wet season. The ice was there, had always been there, and would always be there, by all indications at the time.

Posnansky worked to materialize his skiing fantasy: He hired laborers to build an access road, haul materials, construct cabins, and install the first rope tow at Chacaltaya—powered by a truck engine housed in a cabin hanging over the base of the ski run.

In a recent development, posnansky, along with other mountain athletes, founded the Club Andino Boliviano, a group of dedicated skiers and enthusiasts. To fund the growing ski scene, the club drew involvement from La Paz’s middle and upper classes, and Posnansky and the club persuaded Bolivia’s Congress to pass tax legislation dedicating 1% of the country’s hotel revenue to Bolivia’s Ski and Mountaineering Federation. This funding would help transform Chacaltaya from a passion project into the hub of Bolivian skiing—a hub that, while retaining its roughshod, backyard roots, would grow to host a national ski team, crowded weekend races, the first South American ski championships, and athletes who would represent the country at Winter Olympics.

According to recent reports, when Mendoza was a young boy in El Alto, his family wasn’t connected to La Paz’s urban elite who would drive across the Altiplano to ski. Mendoza’s father, however, worked as the caretaker of Chacaltaya, often living for weeks at a time at the resort to maintain the facilities.

When he was 15, Mendoza accompanied his father to the mountain for the first time. He spent his first night at the base racked by altitude sickness.

It has been revealed that “My dad gave me coca leaf tea,” he says. The next day, “the sun came out; I felt better. I got acclimated, and I learned to ski.”.

Fifty years later, standing once again on the summit, Mendoza is transported back to the resort’s heyday.

Sources indicate that “The rope would drop us off here,” he indicates. “And then …” He puts his hands on bent knees and waves them back and forth in a slalom. He raises his hands over his head and lets out a high yell, feeling the old rush of racing in the cold air.

Mendoza is in his 60s now. He has a harder time seeing, looking out through thick glasses, and his knees sometimes bother him.

Around us the glacier has completely vanished, leaving behind only a mountain of rock.

Infatuated with the world of snow and slopes, Mendoza learned to ski on gear borrowed from Club Andino. He worked long, physical days with his father, tasks ranging from construction and upkeep to manning the rope tow—including rebraiding the wire cable whenever it snapped, a job that left Mendoza with thin white scars across his fingers. From his father, he learned to manage the mountain, the two often sleeping in the lodge for weeks at a time.

Meanwhile, his love for skiing only deepened. Mendoza remembers Stanley Shepard, an American diplomat posted in Bolivia, who taught him advanced techniques and shared the joy of the mountain.

“Stan would drive up this road so fast,” he says as we drive the same route from the city to Chacaltaya some 50 years later. He smiles with the memory of the adrenaline rush.

According to recent reports, mendoza’s ski story exists in a split reality: In one, he is the caretaker’s son, surrounded by a country’s elites who lived near, but not next to, families like his. The socioeconomic divide paralleled the geography: La Paz’s wealthy neighborhoods in the valley, El Alto on the cold outcropping of the Altiplano above. Despite the divide, Mendoza was a vital member of the Chacaltaya scene; the members of Club Andino were his friends. The nights were full of music whenever others would sleep alongside him and his father at the refugio. The period is marked in Mendoza’s mind by shared meals in the cabin and shared runs on the mountain.

Industry observers note that by the 1970s, with Chacaltaya entering its golden period, Mendoza was both employee and skier. He tells me he used to set up for the weekend slalom races—ones he’d often compete in as well. I ask about the slalom poles, curious about infrastructure. He tells me they were made nearby. “But the first times,” he states, “we used hollow canes, like cornstalks.”.

In a 1976 article in Ski Magazine, American writer Jeff Frees described his visit to the ski hill. There were some two dozen weekly skiers sharing the piste and “a slightly doglegged swath of snow” that was “lined with rocks from top to bottom,” although there were no lift lines, he writes.

The chalet, perched on a rocky precipice, was “so frightening and insecure-looking,” that “some skiers refused to enter it,” Frees says. With the altitude nearing 18,000 feet, other visitors didn’t even bother trying, exiting the minibus up from La Paz only to climb into the truck heading back down the road.

This was the electric, eclectic golden period. One 1,000-foot run served by a single rope tow prone to snapping and powered by a truck engine. A handful of foreign visitors and the dedicated group of Club Andino members. A small, warm refugio built on a cliffside, filled with coca tea, quinoa soup, and music. Weekend races and training events for young locals, supporting ski teams who would go on to participate in four consecutive Olympics starting in 1980. And behind this incredible scene was Samuel Mendoza.

In a recent development, “It was frozen all the time,” Mendoza says. “The people said, ‘This is forever. It will never recede.’”.

“But little by little, it started to thaw.”.

Recent findings suggest that scientists had been documenting Chacaltaya for decades, but a systematic study of the glacier began in 1991, led in part by Edson Ramírez of the Universidad Mayor de San Andrés in La Paz (UMSA). Glaciologists’ observations began to echo the concerns skiers had voiced for years: Chacaltaya was melting—and fast.

“Snow would fall at night,” Mendoza states, “but it would be gone by midday.” As temperatures rose, the glacier retreated, exposing more and more of the rock underneath.

While the retreat was evident in some of the earliest photos from the 1940s, Ramírez and his team found that, in just six years from 1992 to 1998, the glacier’s melt had accelerated dramatically, losing more than 40% of its surface area and roughly two-thirds of its ice volume. The team’s prediction: The glacier would disappear within 10 to 15 years.

By 2009, the glacier was completely gone.

“The entire glacier of the world’s highest ski slope had turned to water,” Mendoza reflects.

According to recent reports, as the ski run melted under them, various last-ditch efforts were implemented to keep the sport alive. Artificial snow production was attempted, but ultimately proved too costly. Moving the resort to other nearby mountains was considered, but transportation and access were constant hurdles. Even traditional Andean rituals were offered to the mountain gods.

But the glacier, once gone, would not come back.

In a recent development, without their ski hub, the Club Andino eventually unraveled. A photo hangs in the abandoned refugio of smiling members piled outside the club. Mendoza tells me their names—a running list of friends moved abroad or passed away. Even their headquarters in La Paz is now shuttered.

While sooner than expected, Chacaltaya’s glacier death was not unique within the broader scope of Andean glaciers. Research published in 2026 by Giuliana Adrianzen and Andrew Malone of the University of Illinois Chicago found that Bolivia’s Cordillera Real lost a stunning 42% of its glaciated area between 1992 and 2024.

This trend is widespread across the Andes, which are home to 99% of the world’s tropical glacier area—particularly vulnerable ice fields located near the Earth’s equator.

Industry observers note that glaciers in this latitudinal band are much more susceptible to small temperature changes than those outside of it. Kept frozen primarily by extreme altitude, tropical glaciers already exist close to the temperature threshold to sustain permanent ice; they also don’t experience the long, cold winters of glaciers nearer the poles. Andean glaciers are now thinning 35% faster than the global average, according to a 2025 international report co-authored by researchers at the University of Sheffield. As global warming pushes the freezing level higher, more precipitation falls on these glaciers as rain instead of snow, accelerating the melt.

Over the 60 years between 1960 and 2020, Peru lost 56% of its glacier area. In 2024, Venezuela was declared glacier-free with the death of the Humboldt Glacier (named, perhaps ominously, after the German naturalist who pioneered the notion that everything in the natural world is connected). Colombia is following the same trajectory, having lost more than 90% of its glaciated area since the mid-1800s.

According to UNESCO, the Andes could lose 78 to 97% of their tropical glacier volume by the year 2100.

Recent findings suggest that of course, more than skiing is at risk—including the water supply risk of some 90 million people across the Andes. These glaciers serve as water reserves for the millions of people who live downstream, and their disappearance foreshadows looming ecological disasters. Many Andean municipalities also rely on hydroelectric power, which depends on steady dry-season meltwater from the glaciers. As the glaciers shrink, that flow is dwindling, increasing the severity of droughts.

While Chacaltaya’s lift has long since stopped spinning, a handful of trained guides and foreign clients continue to practice ski mountaineering in Bolivia, climbing high peaks and bombing descents on still-intact glaciers. While the chalet has ceased to function, the mountain remains an active scientific base. The Chacaltaya Observatory, run by UMSA’s Laboratory for Atmospheric Physics—with multiple international collaborators—continues to measure the atmosphere, climate, and cosmic rays.

And although skiing has abandoned the mountain, Mendoza has not.

Since his father died on Chacaltaya over 30 years ago, Mendoza has served as the mountain’s main caretaker, a position he continues to hold. He spends more time in El Alto with his family now, but he and his brother Adolfo still make multiple trips a week to Chacaltaya, welcoming the handful of tourists who come to visit the abandoned chalet or use it as an acclimatization hike. With the small collected entrance fees, he pays for repairs and maintains his memories of the resort.

Many of Mendoza’s days, however, are spent in solitude, standing alone at 17,000 feet on Chacaltaya’s rocky remains.

Industry observers note that “When you’re alone it’s a little sad,” he says. “With only the birds, the condors, the Andean foxes.”.

Recent findings suggest that since the collapse of the glacier, a new group of athletes has taken to Chacaltaya: trail runners—whose arrival is directly tied to skiing’s disappearance. Paolo Choque is the director of skyrunning for the Bolivian Ski and Mountaineering Federation. One of the “last people to learn to ski in Bolivia,” Choque witnessed the collapse of skiing at Chacaltaya, and he has since helped cultivate trail running to take its place.

According to recent reports, in 2001, when Choque learned to ski, the main chunk of the glacier was already “ruined,” he notes. Against the backdrop of the dying mountain, Choque became involved in promoting skiing and snowboarding in Bolivia, including searching for alternative mountains to host competitions.

Sources indicate that in 2011, the federation found another suitable slope at nearby Charquini and hosted a Bolivian Ski Championship. Choque states that snowboarding grew in popularity over a handful of years with the promotion efforts, but participation numbers remained low—with just 25 racers in the snowboard event in 2015. Amid melting ice and low participation, he made the decision to pivot. “I stated, ‘No, this isn’t going anywhere. We don’t even have a ski slope.’”.

In a recent development, inspired by the sport’s explosion in Spain, Choque organized a pilot skyrunning race on Chacaltaya in 2016, which was met with a strong reception. Athletes had returned to the mountain. The federation’s championship now draws about 200 participants each year, according to Choque. Racers gain points at multiple events across the country, which take place over otherworldly terrain—from the world’s largest salt flats in Uyuni to the folds of the Sajama stratovolcano, the shores of Lake Titicaca, and, of course, Chacaltaya Mountain.

“Skiing may have died,” Choque indicates, “but mountain sports have not.”.

It has been revealed that while private trail races have also increased in popularity in Bolivia over the past decade, the federation aims to develop skyrunning and its next generation of athletes through accessible competition. Race entries, Choque emphasizes, are kept inexpensive, and youth competition categories give athletes the opportunity to qualify for international competition.

“For me, sport must come first, and it must be accessible to everyone,” Choque notes.

Despite challenges with funding, Choque claims the federation has seen success in sending participants to compete in the South American Championships, where they have earned podium finishes, including three medals in 2025.

As one sport fades and another grows, Choque defines what success could look like for Bolivian skyrunning.

Recent findings suggest that “What I want to achieve is to bring a South American championship here, and if possible, even a youth world championship to Bolivia,” he indicates. “We have the potential.”.

Paolo and the federation hope that Chacaltaya will continue to be an vital mountain hub for decades to come—with or without the glacier.

It has been revealed that for all of the uniqueness of Chacaltaya’s history, it does mirror a larger global skiing trend: most of the participants were wealthy. Mendoza remembers well the divide caused by the cost of equipment. “From the city of El Alto there weren’t a lot of skiers,” he claims.

Industry observers note that through the Ski and Mountaineering Federation, Choque is determined that the next iteration of Chacaltaya’s mountain sports—trail and sky running—do not follow the same pattern. Mendoza, meanwhile, has seen some of the runners who are taking to the mountain to train where he once skied. I ask him if he would ever run one of the races, and he tells me he enjoys running. His knees, though, keep him from doing too much of it. But when a German tourist wanted to race from the summit to the lagoon below, Mendoza happily mentioned yes.

“Replacing skiing at Chacaltaya in the future is possible,” he says.

Looking across the dry slope where he learned to ski, the rusted remains of his rope tow, the faded chalet and the memories contained, Mendoza takes a deep breath. At the end of the day, as we drive the winding dirt road down to the city with Chacaltaya shrinking into the distance behind us, he looks ahead.

“It makes me happy when people visit the mountain,” he indicates.

#90652. How to Clean Overhanging Routes Without Taking the Biggest Swing of Your Life

How to Clean Overhanging Routes Without Taking the Biggest Swing of Your Life

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4446 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission.
  • Permadraws are incredibly convenient, but sometimes they are not appropriate for an area.
  • So if there are no permadraws, how do you safely clean a steep sport route?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Permadraws are incredibly convenient, but sometimes they are not appropriate for an area. There are a few reasons for this. One is that permadraws are highly visible, turning a natural setting into an outdoor climbing gym. Permadraws also corrode rapidly in marine and coastal environments. Lastly, they are expensive.

So if there are no permadraws, how do you safely clean a steep sport route? Leaving a carabiner is the next easiest solution. But what if you don’t want to do that?

In a recent development, these nagging questions—as well as recent accidents—have compelled me to put together this long list of options for cleaning your next steep line. I’ve organized these methods into three categories:.

Each method has pros and cons in regards to simplicity, speed, and safety.

According to recent reports, ultimately, no single “best method” exists. Though there is a singular worst method: rappelling. Cleaning steep routes on rappel is a huge hassle for the climber, and bystanders on the ground who inevitably have to assist. Your method of choice will come down to the circumstances of each route and your personal preferences on simplicity, speed, and risk tolerance. Many of these methods are best saved for niche scenarios, or rare “if-then” situations. Still, it is best to be prepared with knowledge and equipment for those odd cleaning scenarios.

Below, I will discuss several methods for cleaning on the way up. I choose this approach if a route has a roof or dangerous swing potential or if, for whatever reason, I’m not ready to clean the route on the way down. Cleaning on the way up can take more time, but it brings safety gains. Methods range from simple to complex. If cleaning on the way down looks like a nuisance, just lower down to the ground and deal with it later (i.e., on the way back up).

If the route is well within the abilities of someone in your party, toproping to clean is always a good go-to. Never turn down a free toprope, right?

Challenges with this method arise when the climbing gets hard enough where the climber might fall on toprope, thus becoming stuck in space. If the climber is unable to get back to the wall and decides to lower, then you may end up needing to re-lead the climb to re-clip the draws/directionals, so someone can attempt cleaning on toprope again. This is a huge pain, but I see it very often. Thankfully, there are many methods that can help you avoid this scenario.

Industry observers note that firstly, when someone is toproping to clean, we always say they must promise to get to the top. That way, they won’t leave the rope unclipped from lifesaving directionals. This reminder helps incentivize the climber to “blueprint falls.” The worst time to fall is immediately after unclipping a bolt, when the swing will be the farthest, potentially leaving the climber stranded. If you think you might fall, it’s best to adequately rest hanging at a bolt before unclipping. Only unclip the bolt once you’re ready to charge to the next one.

It has been revealed that what if you get unlucky and fall into space? You can try pulling on the belayer’s end of the rope if it’s within reach. However, this method is usually much less productive on steep topropes than on steep lead climbs. Oftentimes, pulling on the rope will get you nowhere.

Industry observers note that if pulling on the rope is getting you nowhere, the next method is boinking. Usually performed on lead, boinking is a strategy a leader can employ after falling into space and becoming unable to reach the rock or a rope. But it does work (albeit sometimes less effectively) on toprope. It’s also tiring and best for short stretches.

The boinking method is simple, but often executed inefficiently. The belayer takes tight on the rope, ideally, and hovers above the ground, or over an edge where they can hang their full body weight. Then, the climber does a pull-up on the climber side of the rope to create a loop of slack. When the climber rapidly releases the slack, the belayer drops. If the belayer is too low to the ground, they will hit the ground, and usually blame the climber.

It has been revealed that for maximum efficiency, the belayer can easily ascend the rope (using an ascender and their Grigri) the same distance that the climber needs to ascend. This obviates the need for timing the boinking/drops and is far more relaxing for both parties. It’s also far more efficient than the belayer jumping to take at the right time.

An alternative to boinking is climbing the leash, as it’s called by highliners. This is the main method highliners use to climb the leash after falling, but also works identically in climbing scenarios when you’re not too far below your clip. If you’re flexible, place your heel above your tie-in knot, then pull on the rope, until you can straighten your leg and reach high for the wall. Once you pull on the wall or a draw, the belayer must rapidly take in all the extra slack.

Have the aforementioned methods become too tiring or inefficient? Or is there too much rope drag or rope stretch in the system for them to be effective? The next method is for the stuck climber to ascend the rope. If I don’t want to do the climbing again, I’ll usually jump straight to this method since I always have an ascender with me at the crag. If it’s just a short section to ascend, a prusik or other autoblock will work fine. But for cleaning a full route, you’ll thank yourself for bringing a proper ascender or at least nano-trax, to the crag (they weigh nothing).

Industry observers note that if it is too difficult to pull in and release a draw, you can relocate your ascender above the draw, then clip a PAS/draw into the top carabiner of the draw you wish to clean. Slack the rope from your Grigri to unclip the rope from the draw. If you forgot to move the ascender above the clip, it will get stuck here. Begin ascending again until there is a 90-degree angle between your PAS and tensioned rope. The closer this angle is to 90 degrees, the less muscle required to pull in and unclip the draw. When you unclip the draw from the bolt, it stays attached to your PAS as you go swinging.

According to recent reports, sometimes rope shenanigans can get a bit clunky, especially in roofs. If the bolts are close enough together, you can implement some aid climbing techniques as needed. Sometimes it’s easier to ascend via yarding on bolts, and top-stepping in slings than jugging when it’s really steep. Just do whatever it takes to get up there and reclaim those draws! This can be done in a toprope scenario or a jugging scenario, with a slacked rope, or tensioned.

Industry observers note that the biggest error when cleaning steep routes is cleaning on the way down, then taking a dangerous swing low on the route. There are many ways to clean on the way down. We’ll start with the standard scenario, then dive into niche techniques for oddball scenarios.

In a recent development, many routes have an anchor just below the steep climbing. If this is the case, once you finish cleaning the steep terrain, the first step is to go off belay at that anchor and untie. Then pull the rope from above, re-tie in, and re-lower. When bolting routes, I love adding this type of anchor, not only to provide an easier, shorter version of the route, but also to greatly simplify the process of cleaning lower down the route.

It has been revealed that the most common method for cleaning a steep sport route while lowering is to employ a trolley draw (it goes by many names). This draw connects the belay loop to the belayer’s side of the rope. As you lower, you can pull in on the belayer’s line to clean the draws. Higher up on the route, call for your belayer to hold (stop lowering) when the rope below your trolley draw is nearly level. Lower down on the route, you’ll want to stop sooner, just above the bolt.

There are a few methods for retrieving the draws, but whatever you do, be sure to stop and think before unclipping anything.

Sources indicate that the quickest method is to simply grab the wall, pull in (not up) to slack the draw and remove the draw from the bolt. If you can’t grab holds, often you can draw dyno: grab the draw with two hands and thrust in (not up) to momentarily slack the draw to remove it. In either of these cases, it is far more strenuous to remove the rope from the draw since your trolley draw will be yanking you away from the wall when you still have to clean the draw from the bolt. TLDR: If you’re tensioning the trolley, unclip the draw from the bolt.

If those methods aren’t working, go in direct to the draw you are hoping to retrieve. You can clip your PAS directly to the top carabiner of the draw. If using a draw to go direct, clip an additional draw from the belay loop to the lower carabiner of the draw you wish to clean. It’s best to resist the temptation to relocate the trolley draw into a tether draw. Note that if you remove your trolley draw and do not replace it, you could later unexpectedly fall into space or take a dangerous swing.

Once you’ve clipped direct to the draw, you can unclip the rope from the draw you wish to clean, calling slack if needed. Now, unlike other methods, the primary tension is no longer on the trolley, but instead directly on the bolt. Now pull down on the belayer’s rope to assist them in taking. That 90-degree rule applies here, too. Double check that your trolley is in place, assess the swing potential, then remove the draw from the bolt, and take the swing.

Industry observers note that the lower you go on the route, the more potential energy—and extra rope—builds up in the system. If the trolley accidentally comes unclipped for any reason, it can be catastrophic. You could swing and hit a rock or a tree. The extra rope could even cause you to hit the ground. For this reason, as I get lower, I’ll often double-up my trolley draw. Why not?

Industry observers note that now let’s imagine we’ve lowered all the way down to the first bolt. As mentioned, the farther we end up from the plumb line, the higher the potential swing risk. Sometimes it is safe to unclip and take the swing. Other times, you might hit trees, rocks, or the ground. If both parties decide the swing is safe, the climber must first unclip the trolley draw before taking the swing. If you forget to unclip the trolley draw, you’ll drag the belayer along the ground as you swing. Very unpleasant!

In a recent development, if the belayer is firmly anchored you can opt to keep the trolley draw in place to minimize the swing. However, since most sport crags don’t have convenient ground anchors, this option isn’t always possible. Just remember, don’t expect your belayer alone to stop your swing!

If you’re unsure whether a swing is safe, it’s usually best not to risk it. The horizontal distance of a swing is only a small part of understanding the potential impact. A giant King Swing can be perfectly safe, while a seemingly harmless three-foot swing can be devastating. The greater the starting angle of the swing, the more gravitational potential energy the climber has.

Once past the rope’s vertical plumb line (the lowest point of the swing), the climber begins losing speed. However, impact force depends just as much on how abruptly the climber is stopped as it does on their speed. Finally, account for rope stretch, which can increase the swing’s radius and lower the climber’s trajectory. Always make sure your swing won’t put you into the ground or another obstacle!

In a recent development, even if the swing is all air, there can still be a risk of sharp rock cutting the rope. For this reason, it’s best to avoid massive swings if the rope is rubbing rock. Usually, it’s the swing back toward the wall where rope damage is most likely to occur. Ropes cut most commonly from sideways grinding or sliding. If the rope must press rock, I prefer to place the rope where the rock is perpendicular to the rope’s force.

Industry observers note that if a swing looks risky, the safest and easiest thing is to leave a draw or a carabiner. In my 20-plus years of sport climbing, I’ve never left a carabiner, but I do love this method because it’s allowed me to collect hundreds of free carabiners over the years, which I repurpose as lower-offs on anchors.

Sources indicate that besides cost, there are additional downsides to leaving gear. It is annoying to clip a bolt that has a bail carabiner. Numerous reported accidents exist wherein a climber falls after clipping a draw to the hanger over an existing carabiner, causing the draw’s carabiner to break. For this reason, people climbing after you should hopefully know to slide their draw between the carabiner and the wall when clipping.

It has been revealed that on coastal routes, solid gate carabiners will eventually corrode shut, requiring a saw to remove. On the coast, only leave wiregates unless the wall is frequently trafficked. Speaking of difficult to remove, quick links should not be left on lead bolts. They require someone else to stop their climbing to use two hands to clean up after you. They are not cheaper than carabiners, unless you use the cheap hardware store ones that rust over and eventually require a saw to remove. If you must leave something, it must be a carabiner. Buy a stick clip and you’ll get an endless supply of free carabiners!

In a recent development, let’s say we’ve decided to leave a draw. Now just stay connected with your trolley and continue lowering to the ground. The system will experience extra friction with the zigzag in the rope, which is nice. If you want to leave just a carabiner, you’ll go in direct to the draw you wish to clean, slack the rope, and clip the carabiner to the bolt above the draw. Then insert the climber’s end of the rope to the carabiner. Take hard, then remove the draw, and lower.

According to recent reports, with both of these methods, you can still retrieve your draw/carabiner. The fastest, and sketchiest way to do so is to solo up to the first bolt (and back down). If it’s easy climbing and you’re comfortable, it does get the job done swiftly. Otherwise, removing the draw with a stick clip is much safer, and won’t take too much longer.

Now let’s dig into a couple specialized scenarios.

According to recent reports, technically, the advice that follows on reclaiming the quickdraw from the first bolt safely is part of cleaning a route on the way down. But it involves some niche skills. So, let’s imagine you don’t want to leave a carabiner or draw behind on the first bolt. And you also don’t want to solo up to the first bolt, nor do you have a stick clip. If it’s a significant, rounded glue-in, you can do a lower-out off the first bolt. In short, a lower-out is using a length of rope to do a secondary lower that safely equalizes the climber onto the plumb line. The goal here is to cancel out the swing potential, not to lower to the ground, so the belayer should hold tight. Do not lower the climber until the lower-out is complete or you’ll use up more rope on the lower-out than expected.

There are several ways to set up a lower-out. My favorite method? Give myself a huge tail on a figure-8 on a bight when cleaning the anchor. I make that tail double the length of the distance from the bolt to the object I might hit on a swing. When I arrive at that bolt, I go in direct. Then I unclip the trolley and ask my belayer to relocate under the anchor so they don’t swing. Once they’ve taken hard, I pass the extra long tail through the bolt, tension the extra tail, unclip my attachment to the bolt, lower myself out, then pull the rope through the bolt.

Lower-outs can be done with a knot on the end of the lower-out strand or without. Remember, you should always have the knot in the end of the belayer’s strand! Having a knot on the lower-out chord can keep you from lowering off the end and taking a bad swing if the chord comes up short. However, other times, skipping the knot can sometimes be safer (more on that in a minute). This is where stopping and analyzing is key.

In a recent development, lower-outs can be done with and without a belay device. If it is a pure roof or horizontal traverse, I will use a belay device to lower-out as the forces are significant. This also puts a lot of friction (wear and tear) on the hangers, and should be done sparingly. If the angle is less extreme, I often prefer to lower-out by hand without a belay device. With this method, it is absolutely imperative that the belayer does not lower the climber until the lower-out is complete. Otherwise, the force on your hands will go from very comfortable to dangerous.

But, why on earth would I ever prefer not using a belay device? If your lower-out chord is a tad short, finishing the lower-out by hand is often necessary to maximize your reach before letting go of the chord. The most dangerous option is to use a belay device and no knot; the issue being that it is very difficult to lower without your back facing the wall you’re trying to avoid hitting. Additionally, transitioning from lowering with the device to lowering by hand is risky. The safest thing is to knot the end, lower-out with an assisted braking belay device, hang on the device to clear the knot, then finish lowering by hand. If the pendulum angle is mild enough, I’ll skip those first steps and lower the whole way by hand.

If you use the lower-out method, make sure you have extra rope, as well as a knot in the belayer’s end of the rope. I’d recommend practicing lower-outs in no-risk scenarios first to understand the forces. You may be surprised how easy and safe it can be to two-hand the rope. After the lower-out, simply pull the rope to retrieve. If the belayer avoids lowering during the lower-out, the rope friction on the bolt is minimal and wear and tear on the bolt is non-existent. Still, it’s better to avoid making a habit out of this.

According to recent reports, but what if it’s not a fat rounded glue-in bolt? In that case, I’d highly recommend against a lower-out due to the rubbing of the rope on the sharper hanger. In this case, I would do a rappel-out. You’d rig it the same as a lower-out, but you set up your extra tail as a rappel instead of a lower (find the midpoint of your tail). Similarly, the belayer must avoid the temptation to lower.

While you are rappelling out, negligible rope pressure exists on the hanger, but you won’t create any tensioned rubbing friction like you would when lowering. When equalized onto the plumb line, you can pull the rope through the bolt hanger just like before. To further lessen any friction of the rope on the hanger while pulling, flick the tail and pull when the rope is lightest. This way, there will be no wear and tear.

Let’s say you weren’t planning to do a lower-out or rappel-out. Your belayer can toss you the bottom of the lead line to use just the same. Just make sure that before you untie the stopper knot at the end of the line, that the belayer ties a newly introduced stopper knot on their break strand (an overhand on a bight is fine). This requires a bit more rope than the first method, so just be careful.

Sources indicate that but what if we don’t have enough rope for a lower-out and you don’t have the means to retrieve the draw any other way? If the bolt is solid, you can rappel straight through the bolt hanger. Blasphemy! This is clearly a last resort, but if you’re going to do it, you should at least know the best method. Firstly, never lower through a bolt hanger. That creates much more friction on the rope and bolt than a lower-out or pulling the rope after rappelling.

According to recent reports, I personally do not believe pulling the rope after rappelling would cause any wear and tear, especially if it is a fatty rounded glue-in. What about an expansion bolt’s hanger? Recent tests have shown this scenario to hold around 11kN. There is some mild risk to the rope when pulling it due to the sharper edges. Just like the rappel-out, you can flick the end of the rope and pull the rope when it’s lightest. Additionally, having minimal extra rope to pull through the bolt is notable. Rig the rope so its end barely touches the ground.

Recent findings suggest that lastly, avoid this technique above 15-20 feet off the ground unless it’s an emergency scenario because the rope weight will cause more friction when pulling. And of course, this can all be avoided with a stick clip.

According to recent reports, if the bolts are close enough together, it’s often easier to just down-aid the route. The steeper the route, the less I’ll tension the rope. In a full roof with close enough bolts, I won’t tension the rope at all. There’s no need for bulky aiders though. I like to keep a 120cm sling coiled up on a lightweight carabiner permanently on my harness, using draws as a PAS.

According to recent reports, if the route involves a full roof, it’s usually best to just down-lead/back-aid the route. This is the standard method with the massive roof cracks in Canyonlands. If you can bump cams then there’s no need to tension the rope.

However, this article is about sport climbing. What do you do in a pure roof with spaced out bolts? After running into this scenario many times, I find it easier to do a mix of toprope to clean and jugging the rope. I leave my Grigri on the rope, while the belayer belays with their Grigri, sometimes taking in slack, and sometimes acting as a meat anchor. A Black Diamond grappling hook on the bolt hanger allows me to easily unhook the bolt and take the swing.

It has been revealed that speaking of getting creative, let’s wrap up with what will likely be one of the more controversial takes in this article. I’ve often found the fastest, safest (if you pay attention), and easiest (overall for the team) method is for the climber and belayer to both clean simultaneously. I can’t outright recommend it, unless you have a great attention to detail and years of experience with all of the previous techniques, as well as a variety of other techniques. But I’m including it for those climbing veterans who want to help their partners clean faster and easier.

I generally jump to this method if cleaning the lower part of the route on the way down would be a nuisance or dangerous, but cleaning the top on lower is no-problem. First, I tie off the brake strand on my Grigri. Then, in order to lower the climber, I will climb up the route. I go up, they go down. In doing so, they cancel out much of my weight. If the climbing is hard, I’ll just jug up to the first bolt, clip in, and lower them to their next bolt. We both clean our respective bolts at our leisure. The only communication needed is for the climber to call the standard, “lower” and “hold.”.

It has been revealed that the climber should stop cleaning one bolt before (above) entering any dangerous swing potential. Once they’ve hit that point, they just hang in space as the belayer continues to ascend with a mix of free, aid, and ascending as they clean. Of course, the belayer should tie backup knots when appropriate.

Once the belayer reaches that final draw left on the wall, they should double check that they are in fact above the danger swing potential and take the swing. If the belayer is still in the dangerous swing potential zone, they can use their brake strand to perform a lower-out. Then the belayer can lower themselves, and then the climber, to the ground. This method is fast and very efficient. It’s also nice for the tired climber who doesn’t want to clean the whole route. Just go about it very carefully and thoughtfully.

See? Cleaning steep routes doesn’t have to be a huge nuisance. If these techniques are all too much, just remember your safety comes first. Play it safe and leave a carabiner or a draw anytime. Yes, it’s not ideal, but carabiners are much cheaper than broken legs.

The Best Affordable Ski Trips Across the U.S.

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1505 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, skiers and boarders are gushing about El Niño again.
  • While early signs do suggest that an epic season might be coming, we won’t know for sure until frequent storms continue to dump snow.
  • Climate change is shifting weather patterns, making snow forecasts more challenging.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bogus Basin at sunset (Photo: Steve Bly / Getty).

According to recent reports, skiers and boarders are gushing about El Niño again. The 2026-2027 winter won’t involve just any ENSO but a so-called Super El Niño. Potentially the biggest one on record, with exceptionally warm ocean temps on the West Coast hopefully sending a turbocharged jet stream across the U.S. According to my skiing friends, bartenders, and Trader Joe’s clerks, this could become the most memorable El Niño of our lives. Maybe.

While early signs do suggest that an epic season might be coming, we won’t know for sure until frequent storms continue to dump snow. It’s also uncertain where these potential storms may fall, though an El Niño typically sends winter weather toward the southern half of the country. Another question is whether a chance at great conditions warrants the risk of pricey reservations. And let’s be honest, we’ve all been burned before. Especially in recent years.

Climate change is shifting weather patterns, making snow forecasts more challenging. Rising global temps are causing more rain to fall at higher elevations. Meanwhile, skiing mega-corps have acquired most big-name resorts around the country, driving up lift tickets and inviting allegations of price-fixing. Plus, mountain town gentrification and nationwide inflation have skyrocketed the cost of lodging and meals out.

According to recent reports, the estimated expense of an annual weeklong ski trip for a family of four now ranges from around $5,000 to over $15,000! That’s roughly the same budget as a small destination wedding, if you married a latest person every single year. No surprise, last season’s poor Western conditions saw many Americans separating from the ski industry, with winter resort visits reportedly falling 9.1 percent below the ten-year average.

According to recent reports, despite the rising rates, there are still ways to plan an affordable ski trip. As a member of a self-certified band of dirtbag skiers (along with my friends, bartenders, and Trader Joe’s clerks), I’ve spent years chasing powder on the cheap. During winter road trips around the country, I’ve slept inside my pickup cap, searched for seedy motels, earned backcountry turns, and skied lesser-known resorts. Here are a few ideas for budget-friendly ski trips, plus some tips for finding more options on your own.

Colorado is considered the main character in U.S. skiing, typically accruing the most resort visits each year. Many of the best-known ski mountains are here, including Breck, Keystone, Steamboat, etc. The state is home to the two mega-pass conglomerates, the Epic Pass controlled by Vail and the Ikon Pass controlled by Alterra. Full passes cost over $1,000, plus staying in premier destinations often involves eye-popping price tags.

Recent findings suggest that for years, friends and I explored the state with the reasonable but sadly discontinued Rocky Mountain Super Pass Plus. Other seasons, I ventured across the West using the early Mountain Collective Pass (today’s version is pricier but still includes top resorts). We mostly skied the significant famous mountains while learning to stay down the road in cheaper towns. After the corporate-acquisitions era of recent decades, it seemed like affordable skiing road trips might be a thing of the past.

Recent findings suggest that then came the Indy Pass in 2019-2020, which has become an impressive and economical multi-pass focused on independent and smaller resorts. The concept is not just staying further out but skiing down the road, too. Upcoming customers must join a waitlist. In the meantime, glancing at the Indy resort map can lead you to many budget destinations.

Down the road from Aspen, near Glenwood Springs, consider Sunlight Mountain. The smaller acreage means smaller prices, crowds, and stats—yet it still has steeps. Being lower in elevation, you’ll want to watch the weather to catch the best conditions, a sound practice in general.

Further west, at the edge of the Rockies, try skiing off the Grand Mesa at Powderhorn. Instead of Crested Butte, go up the road to the ridiculously high-elevation Monarch Mountain, helpful if the storms are running warm. And far to the south, away from all significant resorts, check out Wolf Creek, known for capturing the most snow in Colorado.

Sources indicate that another way to find bargain skiing is to bypass the famous Rockies or Sierra and aim for lesser-known mountain ranges. This approach was thrust upon me when I left NorCal, where I grew up, and moved to the Midwest for grad school. Later, my wife and I relocated to the Southeast for her professor job.

When it comes to the East, what has been called the “Ice Coast” now supplements or exceeds its natural totals with advanced snow-making equipment. A good example is Western North Carolina. Outside Boone, the fun Beech Mountain is the East’s highest ski resort, with a microbrewery resting atop its 5,506-foot summit. Their weekday 4-hour flex pass is among the best deals in the Southern Appalachians. Meanwhile, toward the northern side of that range, Vermont has several budget options, including Burke Mountain, Jay Peak, and Smugglers’ Notch.

My favorite area in the East is currently the Alleghenies in West Virginia. Now owned by Alterra, Snowshoe has the biggest name, terrain, and associated expenses. About two hours north, an affordable alternative is a trio of resorts around Canaan Valley. Modernized Timberline Mountain has fast lifts, solid terrain, and ski-in lodgings that attract weekend D.C. crowds. Midweek is quieter and includes gift-card rebates.

The valley’s unique outlier is White Grass, an inexpensive ski touring area with 1,200 feet of vert, a mix of groomed and natural trails, and several peaks to skin up and ski off. The middle-ground gem is old-school Canaan Valley Ski Resort, a state park property with a reasonable lodge on-site plus all the best-of-budget features: slow creaky lifts, moderate stats, and mandatory traverses to reach the widespread and tree-lined trails.

Industry observers note that while living cash-strapped in St. Louis, Missouri, I learned to be extra-creative about winter sports. Outside the city, I skied with fresh pals at tiny Hidden Valley. (“Still looking for it,” we’d joke, but we were happy to have anything.) Graciously, the locals shared some surprising options around the Midwest. Chestnut Mountain overlooking the Mississippi River in Galena, Illinois. Sporty Granite Peak in Wisconsin. The lake-effect Mount Bohemia on Michigan’s Upper Peninsula, where a window ticket costs about the same as an early-bird season pass—approximately $100!

Ditching the “biggest-mountains-or-nothing” mindset can lead you to other deals around the country. In recent years, my investigation into the mysterious cross-continental journey of Native explorer Moncacht-Apé led me repeatedly to Idaho. Simultaneously, I was scouting for future skiing around the unsung Snake River Plain, which may fall on the edge of this season’s El Niño storm tracks.

Located on a ridge north of Boise, Bogus Basin is a nonprofit ski area with vast acreage, fast lifts, and solid terrain. That said, its lower base elevation, around 6,000 feet, mandates condition peeping. About 16 miles downhill, the booming city of Boise is primarily a summer destination, meaning there’s usually a glut of affordable lodgings during winter.

Staying in such warm-weather hotspots, including college sports towns, is another way to consistently pull off cheaper ski trips. With this approach, glancing around the Snake River Plain reveals several more budget options. South of Twin Falls, there are two smaller areas: Magic Mountain and Pomerelle. Rising above Pocatello, aka the friendly college town called “Pokey,” you’ll find the challenging wildcard of Pebble Creek.

It has been revealed that once you start searching for winter deals, you’ll discover some pretty fun choices. Along the winding Mt. Rose Highway, there’s a pair of hidden resorts within striking distance of the “Biggest Little City in the World.” Just 30 minutes from downtown Reno, the closest option is Mt. Rose, a local favorite with Tahoe’s highest base at 8,260 feet. The scenery is top-notch, and the higher elevation often leads to better snow.

Everything else is middle-of-the-pack, and, as we’ve seen, aiming for this level is a reliable way to find affordable skiing. The crowds at Mt. Rose are smaller, particularly midweek. The terrain and stats are solid. The pricing is manageable, especially for Tahoe and when factoring in daily specials like two-for-one Tuesday or Ladies Thursday.

The situation is similar at the smaller Diamond Peak, about 15 minutes further downhill near Incline Village. The lakeside views are expansive, though the prices aren’t quite as good and the lower 6,700-foot base means you should monitor temps and conditions.

According to recent reports, for the cost of driving, you can skip expensive Tahoe lodging and usually find ridiculously low winter rates around Reno. I once snagged a high-rise casino room for $30 per night. After the slopes, I stretched my legs under garish neon lights. Before I knew it, I was watching a free acrobatics show at Circus Circus. It felt like appearing in my own chillier version of Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas, except hold the raw ether and swap in the natural high of budget skiing.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Joern Siegroth / Getty Images).

As firefighters continue to battle a nearby blaze, Shenandoah National Park is implementing rigid fire restrictions due to exceptionally dry conditions and heightened wildfire risks going into Thanksgiving week.

In a Facebook post park officials explained: “These restrictions protect public safety given the elevated risk of wildland fires throughout the park. Shenandoah National Park, Skyline Drive and other facilities and services remain open as scheduled.”.

In a recent development, under these fresh restrictions, visitors to the area will have to rethink their cooking plans since they are temporarily unable to build, attend, or maintain open fires anywhere within the park’s boundaries, including in established pits, grates, and in grills. These regulations also apply to picnic areas, shelters, and huts in the park.

These rules also impact backpackers who rely on portable stoves while recreating in the area. Liquid and wood-fuel camp stoves cannot be used within the park until further notice. At the moment, campers can still use canister stoves like Jet Boils and MSR Pocket Rockets.

This announcement came just one day after the White Oak Flat Fire erupted on U.S. Forest Service land about 50 miles southwest of Shenandoah National Park. Since Friday, the fire has grown to 1,800 acres, with 49% containment. So far, 131 wildland personnel have responded to the fire including handcrews, wildland engines, bulldozers and two helicopters. Wildland firefighters are using active suppression strategies to contain the fire. No evacuations have been reported, and a cause for the fire has yet to be released.

The NPS identifies two primary wildfire seasons in Shenandoah that run from February to May and October through December. Wildfires are relatively common in Virginia during the month of November although the frequency and impacted acreage vary by season and seasonal driving factors like low humidity and breezy weather.

Shenandoah park officials expect these restrictions to remain in place until the region receives enough precipitation to reduce fire risks.

Industry News: On Climbing Mount Robson’s Emperor Face Alone

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (862 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that high on the Emperor Ridge of Mount Robson, enjoying lunch in the sun.
  • Industry observers note that there is a cinema up north.
  • In a recent development, this is a film review of sorts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that high on the Emperor Ridge of Mount Robson, enjoying lunch in the sun. (Photo: Anton Korsun).

Industry observers note that there is a cinema up north. Beyond the rising northern star, beyond the Icefields Parkway, and far beyond the chaos and clamor of the Banff Mountain Film Festival—it is built in the image of a gothic cathedral and shrouded in storm. This cinema operates year round. It has no dress code, schedule, or rules on serving alcohol to minors. Inside, every visitor watches their own film: Some see triumph and elation. Others see despair, retreat, or a kaleidoscope of rock and ice before the front doors shut forever and the silver screen goes deathly black. Yet others simply stand alone in its great white hall, listening to the sound of silence and watching mountain ranges stretch to the horizon like limbs of a great white spider.

In a recent development, this is a film review of sorts. In September of 2026 I soloed Infinite Patience on the Emperor Face of Mount Robson. I’ve been asked to write about it. I’ve been asked why I haven’t posted anything on social media or pontificated my radness to the press. Frankly, it’s because I am a rather poor film critic.

There is no doubt in my mind that alpine climbing is more art than sport.

If I were to ask you—how did Usain Bolt run 100 meters in 9.58 seconds?

“Well, he moved his legs quite fast,” you might say.

But can you tell me how Voytek Kurtyka and Robert Schauer suffered up the Shining Wall of Gasherbrum IV (7,925m) in a 10-day sleep-and-food-deprived push? Or how Steve House and Marko Prezelj clawed their way to the summit of the North Twin with one missing boot and two coreshot ropes? Because I can’t.

I sit in awe of the performers on stage as they pull another rabbit from their hats or escape the icy chains of some far-flung north face yet again. The beauty of alpinism is similar to the beauty of theater, dance, and stage magic—an illusion of wizardry brought about by true mastery of the performers.

However, while similar, alpinism and theater are not the same. Climbing has no audience and no stage. Climbing media has both. In recent times it has become too easy to convince ourselves that perception equals participation—that by clicking that “follow” button or watching that film we can stand in the shoes of the artist. But we can’t. Because to believe otherwise would be to mistake climbing as performing art for climbing as performance art. The former is the way the ascent is portrayed in words, photographs, or film. The latter—what was seen, felt, thought and feared in the moment—is privy only to the performers themselves.

It has been revealed that I often find myself wondering about how the way an ascent is communicated influences the audience’s perception of what actually happened. This can range from flying in a big-budget film crew, to more subtle cues, like how a photo was cropped for Instagram, or whether one was shared at all. These words themselves are guilty, although I try to segregate my act of climbing from my act of writing about it.

It has been revealed that my reluctance to share much about the climb stems from a fear that this blade is sharp on both sides—that the audience’s media-driven perception can in turn influence the climber’s own perception of the experience. Much like how the behaviour of quantum particles changes when they’re observed, climbers too, change our behaviour. Our egos feed off validation. Our eye becomes drawn to the viewfinder or to the stopwatch. We feel the presence of the audience cut through the ridgetop wind. We hear their applause over the crash of séracs in the distance.

Recent findings suggest that I watched The Alpinist on the massive screen when it was first released. While I never met Marc-André Leclerc, it left me feeling that much more went unsaid—that the real movie of his life was seen through his eyes only. A movie no one can rewind.

In a recent development, but anything is possible in cinema. In his account of Infinite Patience, Marc-André describes being unable to take a photo of a beautiful sunrise because his camera batteries had failed—“the shadow of Mt. Robson extending forever into the horizon against a red sky.”.

From my sleeping perch high on the Emperor Ridge, I awoke to the same scene. Waves of red and gold crashed against the east face of Whitehorn Mountain while Robson’s summit pyramid shadowed the valley thousands of feet below. Was this movie magic or something more? Feeling as if I was suddenly not alone, I pulled out my phone in disbelief and took that photo. We can’t rewind each other’s films, but sometimes life lets us watch them together.

Nonetheless, I’m saddened to be left alone with my experience. My words are a lousy companion and my photographs are only worth a thousand lousy words. All I know is that I watched my film on the summit of Mount Robson. Where are you watching yours?

Narrower, more fun, and better at handling whatever the mountain hands you.

Dynastar M-Cross 88 Frontside Ski.

Salomon S/Pro Alpha C BOA Ski Boot.

Sources indicate that not sure what the mountain has in store? Grab the M-Cross 88 and find out. This ski bridges carving and all-mountain categories and is designed for intermediates leveling up, as well as confident skiers looking to play. Its 14-meter turn radius is just a suggestion—we found it equally as game in moguls and tight trees as on wide-open groomers. Dynastar’s Hybrid Core 2.0 (wood plus polyurethane) delivers a damp, poppy feel no matter the terrain. “It’s a wicked fun carving ski that’s up for a little adventure off the beaten path,” one tester said. “It coaxes you into a turn and cradles you there so smoothly I was almost rocked to sleep.”.

Some boots turn heads with new gizmos. The S/Pro Alpha C BOA draws attention with what’s missing: the traditional cuff pivot at the inner ankle. Instead, the cuff flows seamlessly into a low-mounted Powerlink plate—smooth, screw-free, almost Silver Surfer-esque. It’s a radical break from overlap construction, and it delivers two big wins: shockingly easy entry for a narrow boot, and an on-snow feel like nothing else in the category. That low Powerlink connection creates a direct line from leg to ski—sensitive and reactive enough that we pushed harder into edge angles, hips dropping closer to the snow than in any other boot we tested. This one’s for skiers who want a snug, locked-in fit and live for the high-performance turn.

According to testers, this is the ski your instructor wants you to have. That’s because the Arcade series’ whole mission is high performance made accessible. The women’s Arcade W 88 pulls it off with a full Titanal layer, a power rail down the wood core, and an hourglass sidecut with a wide, rockered tip. The payoff: excellent edge hold and turn initiation so easy it barely takes pressure to roll onto edge and carve. Its flex spans skill differences too—soft enough for intermediates, strong enough for experts. Groomers are its home turf, but this 88-millimeter-waisted ski held its own in bumps and bashed through crud and chop. It’s a fun, effortless frontside ski that can rip or relax.

Five things every skier and rider should already know—but some need to be reminded.

Two boards and a binding engineered to make sketchy conditions feel like solid ground.

Revamped for 2027 with input from pro rider Nils Mindnich, the Highpath now features a rounded silhouette that floats better in powder and rides switch better, too. Testers loved the ollie power and reliability of its stiff yet lightweight wood core, reinforced with basalt for snap, and fiberglass to dampen a choppy ride. Responsive and powerful without feeling twitchy, it pairs hybrid camber with a raised flat section underfoot, rockered nose and tail, and a quadratic sidecut for toothy edgehold and fluid carves. One tester called it the “most stable board I’ve ridden.” The stiff flex favors experienced riders, and lighter riders may want to size down.

According to recent reports, feeling tentative about the day’s snow or weather report? The Capita Artemis inspires confidence. Camber underfoot, a directional outline, and a medium-stiff wood core reinforced with flax and aramid strips deliver the edgehold and stability to charge through low-vis moguls, launch side hits, and stick solid landings. This deck prioritizes shooting down the fall line at full speed, making it best for advanced riders. Also available in a women’s model.

Bell-to-bell riders and airtime junkies agree: the Union Neo doesn’t make you choose just one riding style. Its lightweight, mid-stiff highback flex brings heel-to-toe stability without the bulk. EVA-padded ankle straps lock in a cozy, hot-spot-free fit. “Good in any aggressive terrain,” one tester stated. “Responsive and strong.” The adjustable baseplate and dual-density bushings soak up everything from overshot park jumps to spring mank, with zero chatter underfoot.

How to proposal a ski vacation that survives a low-snow winter.

These apparel and accessories don’t need sunshine to look—or perform—their best.

Columbia Roffee Ridge Down Jacket.

Industry observers note that the Moiwa is built for mountain mood swings and kept us riding through frigid mornings and stormy afternoons. A two-layer shell pairs nylon made from recycled fishing nets with a PFAS-free waterproof-breathable membrane, while chest and back fleece panels add warmth. The relaxed freeride fit leaves room for two puffies underneath, while pass pockets, pit vents, a powder skirt, and a helmet-friendly hood round it out. It might be overkill for spring skiing, but for resort days during the coldest months, $400 is a score.

Bold style and serious skiing aren’t mutually exclusive. The Slopestar’s flattering barrel-leg design is built on a three-layer 20K waterproof, windproof membrane that handles everything from spring laps to storm cycles. Thigh vents dump heat, RECCO adds peace of mind, and a restroom-friendly side zip simplifies bathroom breaks. Adjustable suspenders dial in the fit, though shorter torsos may find them too long. Introverts be warned: expect lots of compliments in the lift line.

According to recent reports, small upgrades over several seasons have perfected this pant. A fleece-gripped waistband keeps layers tucked, fleece-lined pockets feel heavenly for parking-lot après, and a thigh pocket opens wide enough for a gloved hand to grab a phone or beacon. PrimaLoft Silver insulation handles temps from negatives into the 40s, while ten-inch thigh vents dump heat fast when things warm up. The two-layer waterproof membrane shrugs off snow and sleet. Between the temp range and details, it’s a tough pant to beat for resort days.

Recent findings suggest that don’t let the svelte look fool you—this cropped puffer earns its keep on the hill with 650-fill down and Columbia’s Omni-Heat Infinity lining that delivers serious warmth without the bulk. Pit zips let heat escape, and soft thumb loops, generous pockets, and a dedicated ski pass pocket round it out—all at a price that doesn’t punish you for wanting to look good.

Milky, overcast skies play tricks on the eyes—unless you’re wearing the Bollé Cerro. Even with the sky spitting snow and rain, we could see 50 feet ahead, and the cylindrical lens delivered a field of view that rivaled goggles twice its size. Flow Tech venting kept things fog-free on the soggiest days. The lens is fixed, not swappable, but its category 1–3 photochromic tech covers most light conditions, so you don’t have to fuss with a second lens. And at $150, they’re a good value.

It has been revealed that sleek is the name of the game for packs that stay out of your way—on the slopes and on the chairlift. The 18-liter Nirvana is slim enough to ride the lift without shrugging it off, yet roomy enough for extra layers, a thermos or water bottle, snacks, and avalanche safety tools in their own dedicated front pocket. Whether you’re lapping the frontside or strapping on skis to bootpack a ridgeline, the Nirvana has your back.

Expensive? Terribly so. Worth every penny? Absolutely. Heating elements run all the way to the fingertips, powered by 22Wh rechargeable batteries for all-day warmth. Paired with a pre-curved leather shell, brushed liner, and low-bulk PrimaLoft insulation, they’re the warmest, most comfortable heated gloves we’ve tested. Haptic feedback makes adjusting heat levels easy, and a magnetic cuff charger simplifies recharging.

It has been revealed that carv 2 won’t replace a real instructor, but it comes close for a fraction of the cost. Clip the sensors onto your boots and the paired smartphone app breaks down your turns—what you did well, what to fix next—pulling data from 1.5 billion tracked turns and real instructor technique tips. This season, the system gets a notable upgrade: an AI coach you can converse with in plain English. It’s not cheap, but compared to lesson prices, it’s a smart investment if you’re stuck in blue square land and ready to chase black diamonds.

Night skiing is the sport’s best-kept secret.

Sources indicate that night skiing gets filed under “kid stuff,” something you age out of, like ski school and hot cocoa bribes. That’s backward. True, night skiing will never hand you the best run of your life. The snow’s usually chalky or refrozen, the lift is a single slow chair, and the terrain is lit like a parking lot. But none of that matters.

There’s a specific, illicit thrill to skiing after dark that goes back to childhood: staying up past bedtime on a school night, bombing down a green or blue run in a full, devil-may-care pizza, feeling like you’ve gotten away with something—you’re outside after dark in the heart of winter, and that alone makes it great.

Sources indicate that it also makes you better. Strip a resort down to one run, and you stop sightseeing and start skiing—really skiing. It’s no coincidence that some of the best alpine skiers in the world were built on hills with just one lift and 300 feet of vertical.

Recent findings suggest that if nothing else, it’s the only time you don’t have to wait in a lift line. Call it kid stuff if you want. Clearly, kids know something the rest of us forgot.
