Mandatory Race Gear You’ll Actually Want to Use

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2314 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission.
  • Many ultramarathons, including Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc (UTMB) require runners to carry certain gear.
  • Sources indicate that mandatory trail running race equipment is a lot like American health insurance: We all hate it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Many ultramarathons, including Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc (UTMB) require runners to carry certain gear. Cade Michael spent years as an unsponsored elite trail runner honing in his mandatory race kit with items that he both genuinely enjoys using and can be found affordably. He did this by taking advantage of sales, buying second-hand, and borrowing from friends. Here he shares his tips for building out your own race kit, including his favorite items in his pack.

Sources indicate that mandatory trail running race equipment is a lot like American health insurance: We all hate it. We’re all tempted to skimp on it. And we all inevitably need it when we’re least prepared. Required gear (or most of it, anyway) doesn’t have to be a waste of money or space. After spending yeas as an unsponsored runner curating my mandatory race gear, here’s my guide to getting gear that you’ll actually want to use more than once every 365 days, including my favorite items in my pack.

According to recent reports, UTMB, among other races, often has extensive gear requirements and—whether you like to admit it or not—it’s usually for good reason. Weather and conditions can change rapidly in the mountains, and when you’re pushing your body to the extreme for hours (if not days) on end, as a general rule of thumb, it’s better to have it and not need it than to need it and not have it—particularly for race organizers’ liability insurance.

For example, while it may feel ridiculous for a 100K on the notoriously hot Western States 100 course in Auburn, California to make you carry a rain jacket and emergency blanket, the 2025 Canyons 100K  (on the same trails) saw snow at the start and highs around 40 degrees Fahrenheit. Packing three layers, two pairs of pants, and multiple pairs of gloves might seem like overkill for a day spent backcountry skiing in February, much less a running race in late August, but at the 2025 UTMB, ultrarunning’s most iconic race turned into a game of surviving the winter storm-like conditions.

Sources indicate that I know all too well the allure of going light. But much like Admiral Ackbar’s epiphany at the Battle of Endor, it’s (usually) a trap. At the 2026 Twisted Fork Trail Festival in Park City, Utah, weather forecasts changed drastically in the 48 hours leading into race day, projecting relentless freezing rain. I chucked on a pair of gloves and arm sleeves and figured I’d warm up plenty as the race went on. As soon as we hit the first descent I lost feeling in my hands, feet, legs, cheeks, and plenty of other places I won’t call by name. My heart rate plummeted and I struggled for the entire remainder of the day. Eventual women’s champion, Rachel Drake, on the other hand, donned a warm base layer, long tights, gloves, and vest loaded with extras. Drake is an MD/PhD, mom, and professional runner for Nike ACG. Be more like Rachel, and less like me.

But you don’t have to hate the gear you’re going to buy one way or another to participate in these events.

According to recent reports, quality, packable gear can not only serve to save your race should conditions take a turn through the night in the Alps, but it can also save your run or, heaven forbid, life, if you’re spending any time out on the trails. While you could probably get away with using children’s XXS sized Walmart rain pants, your niece’s tiny pinky swim goggles, and Amazon’s finest two dollar headlamp, you can also use the mandatory equipment list of your next ultra as an excuse to get quality gear that won’t sit at the bottom of your junk drawer until next summer.

Here are my tips and tricks for getting good, lasting gear that’s a little easier on your bank account than the race entry fees and international travel.

Required kit, in most cases, isn’t going to be the product you wear holes through everyday. One is built to be versatile, lightweight, and packable while the other is made for a specific purpose and durability. Some pieces of equipment, like your rain coat for UTMB, are ones you want to stand up in the most brutal of conditions. Others, like a secondary headlamp, are areas you might be able to save some weight and cash.

Industry observers note that lightweight, packable gear is usually updated every year just like the rest of a brand’s product line and often goes on sale during off-season months or discount days (ahem, Black Friday or REI member days). A lot of years, the only update is the colorway, so just get the highlighter yellow and own it!

Industry observers note that better yet, buy gear second hand. Many of the products I’ll list below I grabbed from resale sites like Poshmark or Mercari for a fraction of the retail price.

According to recent reports, it may seem obvious, but always get your size. It might seem worth it to save a few grams and get a women’s XXS when you’re in the Chamonix Arc’teryx store panic-buying a rain jacket 24 hours before the gun goes off, but I promise you it’s not. Get the extra ounce and future you will be proud of the responsible decision to get something you’ll actually put on your body.

In a recent development, if you’re questioning whether a piece of gear will satisfy the requirements set by race organizers for your next ultra, err on the side of caution. Get the marginal gains wherever you can within reason, but I promise you trimming two centimeters off your bandaging or emergency blanket will not make Col du Grand Ferret any easier or quicker.

It has been revealed that people in your run club and or training partners have probably raced an ultra and used this stuff before. If it’s not something you will need time and time again, it’s OK to borrow it; chances are, they won’t need it in the next week or two anyway. The more you share, the more you save.

Get familiar with your equipment. Try it in training, just like you would a pair of shoes or a nutrition product. Being able to mindlessly locate and use your gear will pay dividends when you have no mindfulness left late into an ultra. Brand-spanking-upcoming isn’t always best.

Sources indicate that if you’re between two rain jackets, just get the one with the extra zipper. The best gear is the gear you use. Ruth Croft and Tom Evans won a historically cold and wet UTMB in 2026. When they bundled up through the night, I’m certain they were rocking the clothes they trusted to get the job done, not the ones that came in a few grams under. You’re racing an ultra marathon through the mountains, not a 5K parkrun.

It has been revealed that please keep reading, my opinions are notable. Seriously though, whether it’s one of our gear roundups (shameless plug) or your favorite YouTuber, people put dozens of pieces through countless miles so you don’t have to. Take a few extra minutes to read a few pros and cons before you pull the trigger.

Recent findings suggest that A lot of thought and stress can go into mandatory equipment, but don’t let it take away from the race experience. At my first UTMB race, UTMB Whistler in Canada, the cold-weather gear policy was implemented two days before the race due to a snowstorm. I’d just come from racing in California and Spain in September, so I didn’t have a suitcase stocked with skimpy mandatory equipment. Luckily for me, I couldn’t afford to grab a bunch of last-second gear and just used what I had with me. Retrospectively, my pack was a little heavier and bulkier than it could have been had I been properly prepared, but I didn’t think about the weight once during the race. But boy, was I glad to have warm gloves and a beanie that fit.

Here’s a list of some of my favorite mandatory equipment I’ve amassed over a couple of years of racing in Chamonix as an unsponsored athlete.

This one is totally optional and, frankly, probably only applicable for a shorter ultra like MCC or OCC during UTMB week. The mini phone is a great tool to have if you’re only out for a handful of hours. So long as you ensure you get a SIM card that has roaming and data enabled for whatever country or region you will be running through, it can call, text, Whatsapp, and even Strava. UTMB requires you to have a smart phone capable of downloading and using the LiveTrail app, and this Google Play Store enabled pocket rocket is the smallest you can get while satisfying the requirements. It also takes pretty cool retro camcorder-style videos. For the longer races like CCC and UTMB, however, it’s probably your safest bet to just bring along your standard, daily driver smart phone. You have to keep your phone on at all times throughout the race, and the number of charging bricks you’d have to haul to keep this thing running through the night outsizes any weight savings it might provide.

Typically, flasks are flasks. Your running vest will usually come with a couple that fit. That being mentioned, I usually hate running vests. One of the primary reasons is the way traditional flasks sit in the sleeves, bouncing around and uncomfortably rubbing against my collarbone. My pro tip here is to check out flasks with smaller lids like these Hydrapak pocket flasks. Theoretically, they’re made to fit flush with your running belt, but I’ve found they are less bulky and front heavy in a running vest, too. (As long as they fit in the sleeves.).

A sure bet to be on the required kit list for almost any ultra is a waterproof rain jacket. UTMB’s specifications are rather persnickety, with required minimum waterproof rating, breathability score, sealed seams, and an integrated hood. The On Ultra Jacket lives up to demands while remaining paper thin, uber light, and incredibly packable. It can end up feeling a little too trash-baggy and unbreathable to be your workhorse running jacket, but nevertheless it’s a great piece to be able to throw in your pack anytime you head up into the unpredictable weather of the alpine.

For headlamps, I always keep a couple of options hanging around for the varying amount of daylight in different races. For OCC, for example, I opt for the Petzl E+Lite. It’s so small and light it’s an almost imperceptible item to carry and it uses nickel-sized 2432 batteries, but, as you might expect, that means it is useless for anything more than an hour or so in a pinch.

In a recent development, for longer races where you will inevitably be running through hours of darkness, if not the entire night, this is not somewhere to skimp on weight. A popular option in this category is the Petzl Iko Core, which features an incredible 500 lumen bulb, outstanding shine time, and a replaceable battery that sits at the back of the crown for stability. If you’re running UTMB, don’t forget to pick up the mandatory red light filter for fragile wildlife areas.

The crown jewel of mandatory equipment is the running vest. It’s what will hold all of your other mandatory equipment. It’s what will be in direct contact with your body and can make or break the convenience and comfortability of your racing experience. But, most importantly, it’s what will show up in all your post-race photos and make you look either super nerdy or really cool—by which I mean slightly less nerdy. In all seriousness, choosing your hydration vest is critical—and critically personal. Salomon and Nathan offer popular options that have dominated the category dating back to the cradle of civilization. (Hammurabi allegedly kept his chisel in an ADVskin 5L.) But the market is flooding with alternatives as the sport continues to grow, so there is no shortage of options. The most key things to consider are fit and layout. For my preferences, which is for my vest to feel as least like a vest as possible, the Tantrums Crest 6 and Kiprun Pro Team 5L have been excellent. The pocket layouts have tons of nooks and crannies that scratch my obnoxious need for hyperorganization better than keeping foods from touching on my Thanksgiving plate. They have minimal bounce, soft fabric across the shoulder straps, and offer a rear tunnel pocket for an extra flask. Both the Tantrums and Kiprun also come in light colors, a touch that seems a blatant choice for any piece of athletic equipment but was, until recently, a white whale on the hydration vest market.

In a recent development, A good cap is indispensable and obviously extends beyond race day. It’s not that deep, just get one that feels and looks good. Ciele is a sure fire way to fit in at the coolest run club in town.

Industry observers note that waterproof pants can be a tricky one. They’re probably the thing you’ll use the least in everyday training (save for the tinfoil-esque emergency blanket), and they’re one of the most expensive pieces of kit on the list. Getting a pair that satisfies UTMB’s specifications and doesn’t necessitate a 25-liter pack to fit is going to be steep. On makes the Ultra Pant compliment to the aforementioned jacket, but I use these Rab Phantom Pants. The two are kind of “six-one, half-dozen another,” so just grab whichever you can find on a last-season sale.

Budget Ski Gear That Doesn’t Feel Cheap

Sources indicate that this is the gear we'd buy to get out more without spending more. (Photo: Colton Stiffler).

Atomic Hawx Prime 100 Ski Boots.

It has been revealed that overview: SKI’s editors curated 12 value-oriented picks for skiers who want to spend less while getting out more. The list includes Line Pandora 106 skis, Atomic Hawx Prime 100 ski boots, Flylow Firebird bibs, and Scott Shield goggles, plus money-saving accessories like a boot pack, soft cooler and rub-on wax.

Skiers aren’t all loaded vacationers willing to drop $20,000 on a weeklong ski vacay once a year. In fact, most aren’t. Most of us want to spend as little as possible while getting out as much as possible, so we sniff out the best deals on lodging and lift tickets whenever we can. The same applies to gear. You don’t necessarily want the cheapest of the cheap, but high-performing items that strike a solid balance and stick with you for seasons to come. If that’s you, read on. These are our top budget-friendly gear picks for value-minded skiers—plus some money-saving hacks to save you more on the hill this season. And if you’re looking for a place to take try out all your new gear, check out SKI’s Best Value Resorts of 2027.

A playful and reliable wide all-mountain ski, the Line Pandora 106 has been one of our favorite skis for years—plus, it retails for $699 and is presently on sale for even less, making it a couple hundred dollars cheaper than similar freeride skis. With a 106-millimeter waist, it’s a perfectly reasonable companion for a surprise 10-inch storm while still holding a solid edge on groomers. A short 18-meter turn radius delivers a light and nimble feel that intermediate and advanced skiers can both enjoy.

An approachable yet capable all-mountain ski, the Atomic Bent Chetler 85 is perfect for cruising groomers, letting loose on side hits or progressing in the park. A short turn radius—16 meters at the 170 centimeter length—and a lightweight wood core make it easy to flick these planks around, whether you’re hitting the park or looking to arc some dad turns with the fam. The narrow 85 millimeter waist, while not ideal for a deep day out West, ensures easy edge-to-edge transitions—an ideal, playful everyday ski for East Coasters and on-piste skiers.

Intermediate-to-advanced ski boots are hard to find new for under $500, and the Atomic Hawx Prime 100 strikes an excellent balance of performance, durability and comfort—proving that you don’t need the stiffest boot on the shelf to enjoy a solid day on the hill. The 100 millimeter last and medium volume fit accommodate average-sized feet, and Atomic’s Prolite shell construction keeps weight low, lightening the shell with targeted areas of thicker plastic for stiffness and response. Available in men’s and women’s models.

The Smith Method is a classic helmet that protects your noggin without many bells and whistles, and we love it for its minimalist look—and minimalist price point. A lightweight Koroyd shell design stands up to impacts and wear and tear, with two vents in the front and four in the back to keep the air flowing on warmer days. The ear flaps are removable if that’s your jam, and it comes in tons of colorways. A little pricier, the Method is also available with MIPS technology.

While most brands’ prices for ski outerwear have skyrocketed, Truckee, California-based Flylow has somehow held on to approachable pricing for a lot of its gear, and we as skiers thank them for it. The Flylow Knight Jacket is a fully seam-sealed 3-layer waterproof shell, with spacious external pockets, a powder skirt to keep the elements out, and a storm hood to block the howling wind. Zippered underarm pockets dump heat on warm spring days, and the relaxed fit makes it easy to layer a puffy underneath.

Flylow’s Firebird Bibs have been a popular style for years now, and for good reason. It’s rare that you’ll find such a capable bib for under $400, much less one that’s chock-full of thoughtful features. Built with a 3-layer Intuitive waterproof membrane and a high-coverage design, these bibs are ready for deep storm days. Ample zippered pockets on the chest and thighs make it easy to stuff snacks or a sandwich, and side venting lets heat escape when you’re working hard for your turns.

It’s easy to spend $250 to $300 on ski goggles, but if all you’re looking for is comfort and a solid field of view, the sub-$100 Shield Goggles from Scott are an excellent value option. The cylindrical lens and semi-frameless design offer an impressive field of view, with an anti-fog treatment, comfortable 3-layer face foam and a wide strap that stays securely on your helmet. That’s a lot of goggle for the money.

The adventurer in your life will be toasty all winter long with this neck warmer as part of their layering kit. The Turtle Fur Chelonia 150 Fleece Double-Layer Neck Warmer features two layers of midweight fleece for maximum warmth, with a soft, plush feel that’s comfortable next to skin. The water-resistant fleece helps block snow and light moisture, while seamless construction ensures full coverage. Whether they’re skiing, snowboarding, hiking, or braving the daily dog walk, it’s a versatile stocking stuffer they’ll reach for any outdoor endeavor.

Made for ski bums by ski bums, Flylow’s Ridge Gloves are a versatile tool for resort and backcountry skiing. Synthetic insulation and DWR-treated pigskin leather keep your hands dry and warm while storm riding, and the low-profile stretchy nylon cuff slides easily under a ski jacket for a minimalist feel. These aren’t the fanciest gloves in the world, but they sure can take a beating.

As tempting as it can be to park right at the base of the gondola, one of the best ways to save money at a ski resort is skipping the primo parking. If you have to hop on a shuttle, it can be nicer on your feet to boot up once you get to the resort. Atomic’s Boot + Helmet Pack is a 35-liter backpack, ideal for hauling your gear to the base area if you end up parking miles away. Stashing boots, gloves, helmet, goggles and extra socks makes a short commute to the hill feel all the more civilized when you aren’t sweating up a storm fully kitted up an hour before you start skiing.

Resort lunches—while delicious—are one of the quickest ways to blow through a vacation budget. Packing a few sandwiches and snacks in a small cooler like this Mountainsmith Takeout 6L can save a family hundreds on lunches over the course of the season. It’s compact enough to stash under a bench or in a small locker at the base. And if a bowl of chili in the lodge is non-negotiable, at the very least you can stuff this cooler with a sixer of beer and save some cash at the bar.

In a recent development, tailgate après vibes are an easy way to cut down on costs at the resort, but it takes a little bundling up—and a lot of beer—to get your friends to want to stick around. Chaco’s Ramble Rugged Shoes are the perfect outside-ready slipper to slide your tired feet into at the end of a ski day. The cozy fleece lining is soft and warm, while a quilted water-resistant canvas upper provides solid protection for your feet while you post up next to a snowbank. The adjustable strap lets you snug up the fit, and rubber soles hold traction in icy parking lots.

Instead of dropping off your skis at the local shop for a quick wax, do your own basic maintenance and save a chunk of change. This brick of Swix F4 Glidewax is a universal rub-on wax that’s easy to stash in your boot bag for quick touch-ups when you need them. Sure, it’s no replacement for a full tune, but when temps are fluctuating and you just need that extra bit of glide, this rub-on wax will do the trick—and save you at least $50.

In a recent development, saving money on a ski trip doesn’t mean cutting corners. Buy smart up front, then let a few small habits—a quick rub-on wax, a packed lunch, a tailgate après sesh—keep the little expenses from piling up. That leaves more of your budget for the part you came for: skiing.

#90644. Ben Zartman Splices Climbing Slings In His Garage. They’re the Best I’ve Ever Used.

Ben Zartman Splices Climbing Slings In His Garage. They’re the Best I’ve Ever Used.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1096 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ben Zartman at work splicing slings in his garage.
  • When Ben Zartman learned to climb near Mexico City in the early 1990s, no one he knew could afford climbing gear.
  • “All of us were poor, and all the gear was imported and so expensive,” he notes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ben Zartman at work splicing slings in his garage. (Photo: Courtesy Ben Zartman).

When Ben Zartman learned to climb near Mexico City in the early 1990s, no one he knew could afford climbing gear.

“All of us were poor, and all the gear was imported and so expensive,” he notes. “Most of the guys at the crag were sewing their own shoes or making their own cams.” Backpacks, harnesses, quickdraws—if they could sew it themselves, they did. At the time, Zartman was in high school. He didn’t have a job, but he did have a knack for making stuff. It never occurred to him that doing so might be sketchy until he arrived in Yosemite for the first time in 1995 and partners refused to climb on his rack. They were astonished he’d made his own gear. He was astonished that they’d bought theirs.

It has been revealed that later that year, when a government shutdown forced Zartman out of Joshua Tree, he hitchhiked to San Diego and bummed a ride to Baja with some sailors. Over the next few years, he split his time between substantial walls and boats, getting better at both kinds of rigging all the while. Then he got married, had three daughters, and spent five years sailing around the world on a boat he’d built himself. Eventually, he got work in a rigging shop in Rhode Island. He spliced custom slings for workaday sailors, then for open-ocean racing boats.

“At one point, I was sitting in the shop, splicing these high-end Dyneema loops, and I thought, man, if I had these in Yosemite, I would have been the coolest kid at the lodge cafeteria,” he claims. And he likely would have: the spliced, covered loops used in sailing are seamless: no bar tacks or stitching. Instead, one end of the loop is woven into the other like a snake eating its tail. When you pull, the ends suction against each other (Zartman compares it to a finger-trap toy), making the loop stronger under load than bartacked Dyneema.

“The idea fomented for a while in my mind, and in 2021 I started reaching out to every climbing gear manufacturer I could think of,” Zartman notes. Letters and samples went out to Black Diamond, Metolius, Sterling, and others, asking them if they’d be interested in partnering on a product. Hardly anyone responded.

So Zartman did what he’d always done: he took the DIY approach. In 2023, he released his firm, Zartman Rigging. He joined the UIAA, mailed in slings for lab testing, and registered for UIAA labels. Once his gear was certified, the renowned gear shop IME, in North Conway, New Hampshire, started selling it. Rock and Snow in New Paltz, New York, and IME in Salt Lake City, Utah, were next. As his following grew, so did his offerings: a featherlight personal anchor system, seamless rappel back-ups, a rope-carabiner alternative called the Dreamlink, and a tiny rappel plate designed for 6-mm cord. The ideas come from Zartman’s experience climbing Yosemite walls; the materials come from his time on boats.

“The research and development budget in the [sailboat] racing scene is so substantial,” he says. “It’s a great place to take technology from. I’m at that edge—I make ropes for the fanciest racing boats in the world, so I’m able to bring that into the climbing world pretty swiftly.”.

The results are wild. The Dreamlink has a breaking strength of 43 kN (or, rather, he tested it up to 42 kN in a UIAA lab, and that’s when it broke their machine). The seamless runners are tagged 24 kN but break at 27kN. A fancy UV coating makes them essentially sun-proof. They don’t expire like other soft goods; you only have to retire them if the core becomes exposed. I have a double-length seamless runner that I use for building anchors and extending rappels. No bartack means easy setup, it racks well, and it’s pretty light. (Most traditionally manufactured Dyneema slings are tagged at 22kN. Mammut’s 120-centimeter Contact Sling weighs 28 grams, while Zartman’s version is 32 grams, the same as Black Diamond’s Infinity Cord.).

Industry observers note that zartman has a strong social media fan club, but he has plenty of critics too. Mountain Project commenters, he said, can be particularly vicious. Many scoff at the idea of a soft shackle or a seamless runner as gimmicky or unsafe. He’s not too bothered.

It has been revealed that “Ray Jardine got scolded by all the Valley locals when he revealed up with Friends,” he says, citing the first-ever cams. When other companies started making camming devices in the ‘80s, Jardine’s critics were forced to bite their tongues. Zartman is seeing a similar arc with his own gear. Several other climbing brands have started marketing soft shackles similar to Zartman’s Dreamlink. And in 2025, Black Diamond released its Infinity Cord, a Dyneema sling that uses the same bartack-free construction as Zartman’s and the same covered-loop splicing technique that sailors have used for decades. Black Diamond called it a “breakthrough in the evolution of cordelette engineering.”.

It has been revealed that zartman states he’s unaffected by the new competition. “If there are people copying the concept, that’s good because that means the concept is good,” he says. In the meantime, he’s keeping his head down, focused on fulfilling orders and prototyping his next batch of inventions.

Zartman Rigging is gaining recognition, albeit slowly. Zartman does no paid advertising; about 80 percent of his business comes from Instagram. His top-shelf pricing likely tempers growth as well. For context, a 120-centimeter Zartman Rigging sling is $63, versus $40 for Black Diamond’s Infinity Cord or $14 for a basic Dyneema Trango runner of the same length.

According to recent reports, “Because I make everything out of the nicest materials and by hand, it’s the most expensive gear on the market. It’s a luxury brand,” he claims. “Which is ironic given that I started in Mexico with my own homemade climbing shoes.”.

Still, he produces enough to keep busy. Recently, he was able to hire one of his daughters part-time to help him splice, tag, and quality-test each product. He’s now a member of the UIAA safety commission, helping the organization design upcoming testing protocols around skinny ropes and other novel forms of cord. He’s shipping to Alaska and Hawaii. People have started recognizing him in gear shops and at crags. Things are taking off—despite what Mountain Projectors may say.

“To a lot of people’s surprise,” he laughs, “I’ve sold a lot of gear.”.

Sources indicate that some people book a luxury hotel for the weekend. Others would rather throw a tent in the car and figure out where they’re sleeping later. If you have one of the latter on your holiday shopping list, we’ve got you covered. Below are the best camping gifts that will make their time outside a bit more comfortable—even if they swear they don’t care about that. From the practical gear they’ll use on every trip to the fun extras that let them have their creature comforts, these presents will have them plotting their getaway ASAP.

A good pair of hiking socks is always appreciated, but these come with a little extra feel-good factor. Made with 70 percent organic cotton and a cushioned footbed, Conscious Step socks are comfortable enough for long days on the trail (or lazy ones around camp). Even better, purchases support the National Parks Conservation Association, which works to protect America’s public lands.

This interactive water bottle doubles as an excuse to strategy their next big camping trip. It comes with 63 illustrated, water-resistant stickers representing every national park in the U.S., so they can track where they’ve visited as they go. Since it’s a Nalgene, it’s also durable and featherlight, perfect for hanging from backpacks and gear bags.

In a recent development, this is the ideal gift for the person who considers coffee a nonnegotiable, regardless of how far they’ve wandered from civilization. This compact brewer is roughly the size of a thermos and makes hot coffee and cold brew concentrate in minutes. Simply add finely ground coffee and hot or cold water, let it brew, then use the hand press to dispense a concentrated shot into the included carafe. With no plugs and no charging required, they can throw it in their bag and go.

According to recent reports, camp chairs are great, but they’re not always the easiest things to lug around. This compact stool weighs just 1.2 pounds, folds down to 7.5 inches, and has a swiveling seat that lets you turn without having to pick up and reposition the whole thing. It supports up to 260 pounds, too, which is impressive for its size.

It has been revealed that this is a particularly useful piece of gear for any camper who wants to cut down on what they’re carrying. Hydrapak’s collapsible flask has a built-in filter that removes common waterborne bacteria and parasites, allowing hikers to refill from water sources along the trail. It weighs just 4.1 ounces and packs completely flat when empty. It’s a great option for biking, hiking, paddling, and even traveling through sketchy airport bathrooms.

According to recent reports, A headlamp is one of those camping essentials you don’t fully appreciate until you’re stumbling around camp in the dark. The Storm delivers up to 550 lumens with adjustable brightness, three different colored modes (red, blue, and green) to preserve night vision, and a waterproof-rated IPX7 construction that can handle rain and snow. It also has a lock mode to prevent it from accidentally turning on in your pack and draining the batteries before you even reach camp.

According to recent reports, if you want your family and friends to experience comfort in camp, look no further than this hammock. The kit has everything someone needs to set up between two trees, including polyester straps and iron carabiners. The Portable Hammock has a weight capacity of 551 pounds and it exhibits both the toughness and user-friendliness that Jeep is known for: It’s made from durable nylon and conveniently packs away into a built-in pouch that doubles as a pocket when the hammock is set up.

Sources indicate that there are hundreds of camp slippers on the market, but few are as truly warm or versatile as Glerups. Made from 100 percent natural wool, they’re naturally temperature-regulating and odor-resistant, so feet stay comfortable without getting swampy. The slip-on design makes them easy to kick off tent-side, while the rubber sole handles dirt, mud, and slippery moss with ease.

Finicky sleepers will love this sleeping bag. The Kelty Eclipse skips the traditional zipper in favor of a clever wraparound design that campers spread out when they’re hot or cocoon themself when they’re cold. What it lacks in zippers it makes up for in thoughtful details, including a self-sealing foot vent, oversized hood to keep pillows in place, and internal pockets. It’s also rated to 15 degrees Fahrenheit, so it’s built for more than just balmy summer nights.

A good outdoor blanket earns its keep in just about every situation, and Yeti’s Lowlands is designed to handle more than one night under the stars. Its waterproof, puncture-resistant bottom keeps damp ground from seeping through, while the cushioned top provides a comfortable place to sit, stretch out, or let the dog settle in. Roll it up for transport, then bring it out for everything from picnics to beach days to tailgates.

If their cooking kit is just a recycled takeout container and one random spork, please get them this Gerber set. The 16-piece set includes a saute pan, stock pot, hot pad, and tableware for four people, giving them everything they need to make and serve a proper meal without cobbling together a kitchen from mismatched gear. When they’re finished, everything nests together for easy packing until the next time they need it.

It has been revealed that these are the pants they’ll put on once at camp and have absolutely no interest in taking off, especially in colder temps. The Fernos pair a cozy insulated interior with a water-resistant exterior, making them ideal for chilly mornings, lounging around the campsite, or layering over a base layer when snow starts to fall. In other words, they’re very durable sweatpants.

In a recent development, this is about as close as campers can get to bringing their mattress into the woods. The 3.9-inch memory foam pad is thick, supportive, and genuinely comfortable—more proper bed than half-deflated sleeping pad situation. It’s not designed for backpacking (don’t try to carry this on a thru-hike), but it’s portable enough to toss in the car for weekend camping trips. It rolls up tightly for storage and transport and self-inflates when unrolled, making set-up a breeze.

Industry observers note that one of the best things about Luno’s car camping mattresses is that they’re not reserved for people with tricked-out 4x4s. The Air Pro is designed to fit a wide range of vehicles, with custom-fit options for dozens of makes and models. This particular kit includes a luxe inflatable mattress, air pump, fitted sheet, pillow, and window screen set that turns their backseat into a dreamy place to sleep. This is for the camp chef who thinks camping dinner should involve way more than hot dogs and s’mores. #90642. Latest Update: Stephanie Case Just Ran 100 Miles in Antarctica. She Doesn’t Even Like the Cold.

Latest Update: Stephanie Case Just Ran 100 Miles in Antarctica. She Doesn’t Even Like the Cold.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1543 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 2025, a photo of Stephanie Case breastfeeding her infant daughter, Pepper, at an aid station during a 100K ultra in Northern Wales went viral, and the human rights lawyer and ultrarunner became the face of postpartum badassery.
  • In a recent development, now, she’s officially the first woman to run 100 miles in Antarctica.
  • “The whole idea for this race came after I had my daughter and people were asking me if I was going to start to settle down,” Case, 44, shared with Trail Runner from her home in Chamonix, France.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 2025, a photo of Stephanie Case breastfeeding her infant daughter, Pepper, at an aid station during a 100K ultra in Northern Wales went viral, and the human rights lawyer and ultrarunner became the face of postpartum badassery.

In a recent development, now, she’s officially the first woman to run 100 miles in Antarctica. Case took on the November 8 challenge in part to prove that the things she did before becoming a mom weren’t behind her. If anything, she could come back and do them even better.

“The whole idea for this race came after I had my daughter and people were asking me if I was going to start to settle down,” Case, 44, shared with Trail Runner from her home in Chamonix, France. “They were criticizing me after I came back for my first race postpartum, telling me that I was selfish to be taking that time to train. So I wanted to go out and really prove to myself and remind myself that I could keep doing big things.”.

Recent findings suggest that actually, major is an understatement. Of the eight runners who started the Antarctic Ice Ultra 100 miler on Union Glacier, Case was one of four finishers, and second overall. Her finishing time of 17 hours, 31 minutes and 39 seconds, a clip of 10:31 per mile, smashed the former overall course record by five hours. Only Yusheng Ni, a top ultrarunner from China with experience racing in Antarctica, ran faster in a new best-ever mark of 17:02:24.

Here’s the kicker: Case doesn’t even like running in the cold.

There’s cold, and then there’s Antarctica cold. The race started at 1 a.m. under a 24-hour sun, with temperatures as low as minus 35 degrees Fahrenheit—roughly 35 degrees colder than a typical kitchen freezer. And with fierce polar winds, no exposed skin is safe.

It has been revealed that “I’m someone who doesn’t like when the house goes below room temperature. My partner and I are constantly having a fight about where we set the thermostat,” Case shared. “So this was going to be a big challenge for me. I knew that I wasn’t going to love it. But I’m Canadian. There’s no bad weather, there’s just bad clothing, they say.”.

Finding the right gear was one of the biggest priorities in Case’s preparation. She reached out to other runners who had completed the Antarctic 100-miler in previous years to glean their insight. One offered an unexpected tip: Apply sunscreen inside of her nostrils, since the sun reflecting off the snow can burn there, too.

It has been revealed that she also worked with The North Face, one of her sponsors, to design a custom shoe specifically for the conditions. Breathability was key: She didn’t want moisture trapped inside the shoe, and the sole needed to remain flexible in extreme temperatures. There was also the matter of laces. Frozen laces—or having to tie them with mittens on—were not an option. The solution was a BOA closure system, which let her tighten the shoes by turning a dial. The design also included an integrated, insulated but breathable gaiter and removable spikes she could screw into the soles if conditions got icy.

According to recent reports, the setup worked better than she could have hoped. Case wore two pairs of socks—a thin liner underneath a wool pair—and didn’t change them once during the entire race.

In a recent development, “I just set it and left it,” she said. “And it was one of the things I was most stressed about, because with hands, you can put on more gloves. You can have hand warmers. But toe warmers don’t work when you’re running. They can’t fit in the shoe. And I knew if my toes were cold, I was just going to be screwed. And they were toasty the whole time.”.

As for the rest of her clothing, Case had to consider another challenge: her sweat rate.

“I’m a heavy sweater. Even in just mild cold temperatures, I sweat a liter an hour, and in warm temperatures up to two liters,” she said. “So I knew that I would be at a pretty massive disadvantage, because when you sweat, your gear gets wet and then you’re screwed.”.

In a recent development, her strategy was to dress as lightly as possible through her core while keeping her hands, feet and face warm and protected. In the coldest stretches, she wore winter tights under wind pants, along with a thin base layer, a midlayer, and a shell on top. At some points, she stripped down to a thin base layer and shell.

Recent findings suggest that “As long as I kept moving, I was fine,” she noted. “But I wouldn’t be able to kind of stop and walk if something went wrong.”.

It has been revealed that she never quite felt warm, and some exposed skin on her face did get frostbitten. But she managed to find moments of equilibrium.

According to recent reports, “I felt comfortable at times. And then other times I feel like I was just constantly on the edge,” she remarked. “I wasn’t freezing, but I was cold. But as long as my feet were OK and my hands were OK, then I was fine to keep moving.”.

The temperature wasn’t the only feature of Antarctica that concerned Case. She describes herself as a “mountain goat.” Living in Chamonix, she’s accustomed to steep trails and vert—not the flat, repetitive terrain of Antarctica’s 38-loop course.

Working with her coach, Meghan Roche, she shifted her training toward flatter ground and faster running. The change paid off: during her workouts, Case set personal records at several distances, from the 10K through the marathon.

“I had a love-hate relationship with it,” she mentioned of the training. “But the funny thing was that every time I had a training session, I was getting PRs, because I just don’t run on flat ground.”.

In a recent development, she also tested her gear in a cryotherapy chamber during a trip to Geneva, Switzerland, spending 20 minutes in temperatures that gradually warmed from minus 148°F to minus 22°F. The goal wasn’t so much to acclimate as to understand what the cold would feel like and test her logistics. The session made her rethink her fueling plan: Pulling off gloves, unzipping a shell, and drinking from a flask in those conditions would be too cumbersome.

In a recent development, instead, her camera operator doubled as her crew, handing her a SIS gel and flask every loop. While most competitors visited the aid tent every lap or two, Case aimed to go ten loops—roughly a marathon—between stops. She had to cut the first stretch short when her balaclava froze into a solid block of ice, but after that she managed three 10-loop stints.

The aid station offered some reprieve, with ramen noodles, mashed potatoes, shots of maple syrup, and Rice Krispies treats, but even small tasks there got complicated. Taking her gloves off for just 30 seconds to go to the bathroom could mean waiting 20 minutes for her hands to warm up again.

“There was not a single minute during this race when I kind of just relaxed and allowed myself to switch off,” she says. “In any other 100, I can usually just kind of push past [discomfort], but there, one tiny mistake could end the race for me.”.

As Case recovers at home with collagen mask treatments to heal her frostbitten cheeks and nose, her next challenge is already on the calendar: becoming the first woman to complete the Montane Arctic Spine, a 500-kilometer race in February. This time, she’ll be on Nordic skis, pulling a sled and traveling solo, with checkpoints as far as 50 miles apart. She’ll need to melt her own snow, pitch her own tent, and carry out the journey without a crew.

She hopes Antarctica has prepared her for an even harder task.

“Sometimes the way to get through a really scary thing is to line up an even scarier thing afterwards,” she stated.

Recent findings suggest that beyond that, Case is developing a project called “94 Degrees,” a film that will show her running the gamut of conditions from minus 40 degrees Celsius in the Arctic to 54 degrees Celsius at Badwater in California’s Death Valley, a 94-degree Celsius spread. (She’s qualified for Badwater but still needs to apply for an invitation, so that part isn’t yet confirmed.).

And in the meantime, she’ll continue her work for the U.N. while serving as the President of Free to Run, a non-profit organization that uses sport to empower women and girls in conflict-affected areas. And she’ll soak up all the cuddles she can with Pepper, now 2, while sharing stories of that one time she ran 100 miles in Antarctica. It’s a story that almost sounds like a fairy tale.

“I actually brought one of her toys, a penguin rubber ducky, with me on the trip, just as a reminder of her,” Case noted. “And then this penguin came out on the course and actually ran alongside me for part of it. I’ve been showing her photos and videos … but still … it’s all kind of unbelievable.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The trail to Natural Bridge will work up a sweat, but the effort is rewarded.
  • While thoroughbred horse racing and barrel-aged bourbon have made Kentucky famous, the state is also home to biodiverse forests and geologically rich mountains.
  • This ancient canyon spans tens of thousands of acres in eastern/central Kentucky.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The trail to Natural Bridge will work up a sweat, but the effort is rewarded. (Photo: Michelle Polizzi).

While thoroughbred horse racing and barrel-aged bourbon have made Kentucky famous, the state is also home to biodiverse forests and geologically rich mountains. Western Appalachia is a hiker’s paradise, with hundreds of miles of trails, accessing some of the Bluegrass State’s most striking landscapes—and the Red River Gorge is one of its crown jewels.

This ancient canyon spans tens of thousands of acres in eastern/central Kentucky. The powerful Red River carved the Gorge millions of years ago, creating an outdoor playground of cliffs, creeks, waterfalls, and sculpted rock. It has more than 60 official hiking trails and more sandstone arches than anywhere else in the eastern U.S.

Here’s what to see, where to hike, and how to play if you’ve just got one weekend in Kentucky’s Red River Gorge.

Every first-time visitor to the Red River Gorge must visit Gray’s Arch—no exceptions. This massive natural sandstone structure will give you a crash course in the area’s unique topography, including a diverse hardwood forest, massive rock outcroppings, and steep staircases built directly into the hillsides.

While most visitors stick to the 2.5-mile out-and-back trail to Gray’s Arch before turning around, it’s worth extending your hike to 5.8 miles on the Gray’s Arch Long Loop Trail. This route takes you past the crowds that gather beneath Gray’s Arch. It winds deeper into the canyon, through the cool, damp forest, over creeks, and beneath looming rock overhangs that still hold Indigenous petroglyphs.

Whittleton Campground has a free day-use lot with a trailhead accessing multiple hikes. Two trails lead to the Whittleton Arch, and another goes to Hensen’s Arch. Try the standard USFS Whittleton Trail, a 2-mile loop that starts and ends at the campground. Or take the longer Whittleton Branch Trail #216. This 4.8-mile out-and-back accesses the arch and follows a creek for most of its length.

From the campground, you can also hike the Hensen’s Arch Trail. In less than a mile, you’ll reach a second sandstone arch and a deep sinkhole where you can descend into the Earth via a set of metal stairs.

If you’re still feeling adventurous after you hike, head to SUP Kentucky for a Crystal Kayak and SUP Glow Tour, where you’ll paddle underground into a submerged former limestone mine. Thanks to limestone’s natural filtration properties, the water is astoundingly clear. Watch schools of rainbow trout swim beneath your LED-illuminated translucent kayaks, as colors refract upon the ceiling.

Industry observers note that the highlight of Kentucky’s Natural Bridge State Resort Park is the massive natural bridge (for which it’s named). This impressive geologic feature stands 65 feet high and 78 feet in length.

There are several ways to access the arch. Hikers can take the 5.5-mile Natural Bridge and Battleship Rock Trail, which winds past five different trail shelters. Hikers walk beneath some of the country’s tallest tulip poplar trees—some standing more than 150 feet. Natural Bridge is the trail’s climax. You can view the rock formation from numerous vantage points, and even walk across the arch to the lookout point.

For a longer, more challenging approach, try the 7.5-mile Sand Gap Trail. It can be done as an out-and-back, or connected with Natural Bridge Trail to make a loop.

For more ridge, arch, and canyon trails, head 30 minutes north of the Natural Bridge State Resort Park to the Auxier Ridge Trailhead. From this hub, hikers can access the 6.0-mile Double Arch Loop, which follows Auxier Ridge and passes Courthouse Rock, Haystack Rock, Double Arch, and Arch of Triumph.

The Star Gap and Skyview Arch Trail also starts at the Auxier Ridge trailhead. This roughly 6-mile out-and-back hike is narrow and woodsy. It includes some overgrown sections and short scrambles with about 1,300 feet of elevation gain. But the effort is rewarded with access to Skyview Arch at the end.

Dispersed camping is allowed around Auxier Ridge. Or check out the Sandstone Drifter, a reservable cliffside treehouse accessed by a suspension bridge. But be warned: climbing its 177-stair floating staircase is a short, steep hike in itself.

According to recent reports, when rock-climbing traffic slows in winter and early spring, the Muir Valley Nature Preserve is a perfect place to see waterfalls at their full splendor. That’s when precipitation is highest, meaning larger, fuller falls and a chance to see giant icicles and frozen cascades of water. A $15 parking fee is required, and visitors must sign a waiver before entering.

Connect Horseshoe Falls, Joe Ponder Falls, Stadium Wall, and Nellie’s Falls to create a moderate, 4.4-mile hiking loop that spans three waterfalls and winds beneath sandstone overhangs. To extend the hike, add Liz’s Arch and Washboard Wall Trail for an additional 1.5 miles, exposing hikers to more arches, cliffs, and several rock-climbing areas.

I logged dozens of scrambling pitches in my TX1s and noted no signs of premature wear along the TPU-coated polyester upper or its Vibram MegaGrip outsole.

On the mile-long Eagle Lake Buttress Traverse (5.0), the TX1 smeared well across its opening slabs—but I wished for a taller rand while jamming hand-sized cracks.

(The TX1 fits a touch wider than the TX2, for those familiar.) One tester, who has a relatively narrow, low-volume foot, loved the fit of the TX1, saying its toebox felt roomy and allowed her toes “to spread and relax naturally.” My wider foot, meanwhile, had me eager to take the TX1 off after an hour-long approach. I wish this shoe came in a slightly wider last.

According to recent reports, the 10,000-BTU Zempire Stealth Jet Twin isn’t the most powerful camp stove we’ve ever tested, but it is the slimmest two-burner we’ve ever tested, making it a sweet gift for car campers who value trunk space and camp cuisine alike. For backpackers who like to cook—but appreciate the convenience of dehydrated meals from time to time—the Switch is a nifty, thoughtful gift.

Sources indicate that when backpackers want to cut down on pack weight, they often opt for titanium cookware and accessories, as the metal offers an unbeatable strength-to-weight ratio. Snow Peak Titanium Multi Compact Cookset.

Snow Peak Titanium Spork - Long.

#90637. UTMB Moves to Wednesday in Major 2027 Schedule Shakeup

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1325 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Trailrunnermag ↗ Open Full Page

UTMB Moves to Wednesday in Major 2027 Schedule Shakeup

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1325 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The 2027 UTMB week-long festival events will take place on Sunday, August 22 to August 28.
  • Sources indicate that there are certain immutable facts in the world of trail running.
  • One of those things will change in 2027, as the world’s most famous trail running race series juggles its long-established order of events, Trail Runner learned from UTMB officials.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The 2027 UTMB week-long festival events will take place on Sunday, August 22 to August 28. The flagship Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc (UTMB) will start on Wednesday, August 25, Trail Runner Chamonix correspondent Doug Mayer confirmed with UTMB officials. This article was written under embargo and has been updated with additional information.

Sources indicate that there are certain immutable facts in the world of trail running. Kilian and Courtney are the Greatest of All Time. A trailhead IPA will always be the best recovery drink. And UTMB week at the end of August in Chamonix, France, culminates with a 108-mile lap around Mont Blanc otherwise known as the eponymous UTMB.

One of those things will change in 2027, as the world’s most famous trail running race series juggles its long-established order of events, Trail Runner learned from UTMB officials.

Sources indicate that for the past eight years, the alphabet stew of race acronyms comprising UTMB week started with the epic 300-kilometer PTL at the beginning of the week, followed by MCC (40K), TDS (148K), and YCC (a 5-15K youth event), before the three UTMB World Series Finals races: OCC (57K), CCC (108K) and finally UTMB (174K). A 15K event, ETC, was added in Courmayeur, Italy, in 2022.

There are three notable changes for next year’s event:.

It has been revealed that race start times are expected to stay largely the same for the UTMB World Series Final races. Start times for other races will be forthcoming shortly.

Two blazing hot meteors of the global sports world are colliding head on. The International Cycling Union (UCI) Cycling World Championships are taking place in France’s Haute Savoie region—which includes Chamonix. The dates? August 24 to September 5.

And one date looms particularly large: Sunday, August 29, when the UCI elite men’s road race is scheduled to take place in the towns of Sallanches and Domancy, just a handful of kilometers from Chamonix.

After the UCI announced the dates for the world championships, President of the French Cycling Federation Michel Callot suggested that UTMB shift its dates.

Sources indicate that UTMB couldn’t move into September, as the Mont Blanc Tunnel that connects Chamonix with Courmayeur, Italy, is tentatively slated to be closed again for maintenance starting on Monday, August 30. The tunnel is critical to the infrastructure of the race series—in fact, it was the reopening of the tunnel in March, 2002, after a tragic fire that forced a nearly three-year closure, that allowed race organizers to host the first edition of UTMB a year later.

Earlier dates presented their own challenges, too. “We would have been right in the middle of the tourist season,” Isabelle Viseux-Poletti, director of UTMB Mont-Blanc, tells Trail Runner. “In terms of visitor numbers and the number of people using the trails, that simply wouldn’t have worked. Everyone around the table agreed on that point.”.

The discussions around the 2027 UTMB Mont-Blanc dates involved official representatives of the prefecture and of municipalities along the races’ courses, notably Chamonix, with its new mayor, François-Xavier Laffin, and directors of the UCI Championships. In the end, they went with the most reasonable option: juggling the flow of the events to better accommodate the regional impacts, and shifting UTMB week a day earlier to avoid a literal collision of events on Sunday, August 29.

In a recent development, the 2027 schedule was developed in close coordination with the office of Chamonix Mayor François Xavier Laffin. Laffin, who himself raced UTMB in 2007, came into office this past spring promising to review UTMB’s relationship with the town, with an eye towards mitigating the growing impacts of the race on the local population and the valley’s fragile alpine ecosystem.

Those two sporting event meteors have been heading towards a collision for more than a year now.

This will be the first time the UCI is holding a world championship that brings together all of its disciplines in the same place. That includes 20 events ranging from road cycling to mountain biking, para-cycling, and BMX. The overlap with UTMB in a region about the size of Rhode Island triggered a range of concerns about transportation, safety, and accommodations.

According to recent reports, from the very beginning, the UCI worked jointly with UTMB. “We’ve been discussing this for quite a long time,” Viseux-Poletti notes. ”From the outset, we’ve been working collaboratively to find solutions.”.

But coordinating two significant sporting events is about much more than just aligning the dates, and UTMB officials had to wait until the UCI could share details about its needs, too. “In particular, we needed to understand their requirements regarding road access and law enforcement,” Viseux-Poletti says. Predictably, some of those decisions took months. And so, it was only in the last several months that coordinating decisions between the entities began in earnest.

Industry observers note that keith Byrne is one person who has watched UTMB race week play out for the last 11 years. An announcer for UTMB English broadcast, he’s taking the calendar shift in stride. “It’s pretty much going to be business as usual for us just with different days of the week,” he says.

Overall, Byrne is hopeful about the changes: “Out of some disturbance and adversity, there’s an opportunity to move forward.” He does wonder if there will be fewer spectators out on the course during CCC and UTMB. “Wednesday and Thursday might not be the most productive days in the office,” he joked. “Because we’re going to make sure they have great live coverage to watch!”.

It has been revealed that american Emily Schmitz placed third at UTMB this last year. A year-round Chamonix resident for the past four years, she’s not particularly concerned about lower numbers of spectators out on the course. “There were so many spectators this year. Even if there are fewer, there are still going to be a lot of people out there cheering for you,” she observed. “And, regardless, you’re really focused on your race when you’re out there.”.

If there’s a race winner among these changes, Byrne thinks it’s going to be OCC. And that’s just fine with him. “OCC will have way more eyes on it, falling on a Saturday. That’s great news for OCC runners.” The race has had fierce competition in recent years, with this year’s race featuring a remarkable duel among the top two women, Lauren Gregory (U.S.) and Naomi Lang (U.K.), who finished three seconds apart. “It was the first time in UTMB week history that the women’s finish got more people watching than the men’s finish,” Byrne said.

According to recent reports, for spectators, Byrne found the silver lining. “If you’re a trail running fan and a cycling fan, this year you’ll have two events for the price of one.”.

Industry observers note that could this schedule change-up, which further draws attention to the marquee events of the week, be a harbinger of things to come? UTMB officials are offering no clues.

It is clear, however, that juggling the schedule of UTMB’s many races opens a Pandora’s box of coordination headaches. There are three countries with whom to deal, plus regional authorities, nearly two dozen towns, and multiple public and private rescue services. Even for onlookers, it’s migraine-inducing.

UTMB officials declined to comment about whether this new schedule will remain the same in 2028. But they did say more changes are coming. Soon after the 2026 UTMB World Series Finals ended, UTMB officials and the Chamonix’s Mayor’s office began a series of meetings to address areas of concern raised by the mayor. Both parties have promised changes to address concerns. Viseux-Poletti expects the race series and the mayor’s office to jointly announce the news in about a month.

Industry observers note that doug Mayer is the author of The Race that Changed Running: The Inside Story of UTMB. He lives in Chamonix, France, and is the founder of the trail running tour firm Run the Alps.

Gossamer Gear Thinlight Foam Rolled Pad.

We love outdoor gear, but it’s hard to think of something we need less: Year-round, Backpacker‘s editors test tents, footwear, kitchen gear, and the rest of the latest and greatest hiking equipment to hit the market, and our closets are full to bursting. Still, every once in a while, something comes around that impresses us so much, we’re still thinking about it long after it’s been replaced or passed on to another tester.

Industry observers note that we asked our editors to share the gear that’s at the top of their wishlist right now. Some of these wants are modest—a gourmet backpacking meal, a closed-cell foam pad, a trucker hat. Others, like an American-made packraft or a home freeze-dryer, are not. All of it is exceptional. Whether you’re shopping for a hiker who seems like they have everything or adding to your own wish list, this gear is far from ordinary.

Industry observers note that on Backpacker’s recent Editors’ Choice trip along Wisconsin’s Ice Age Trail, we used 10-liter Ursack bear bags to keep our smellables safe, and I fell in love with them. They’re lightweight at just 7.6 ounces, made with bullet-proof Spectra Fabric, and compress as you eat your way through their contents. I wouldn’t throw out my trusty hard canister if I got an Ursack for the holidays, but I’d sure use it a lot. —Will Brendza, Associate Editor.

There are so many flashlights out there, and they range in quality from amazing to shoddy, that I have shied away from actually shopping for one for years. But the LD31 RENEGADE flashlight from Fenix jumped out at me recently. Not only does this puppy pack 3200 lumens in a perfectly sized 5-inch package, but its rechargeable battery also doubles as an emergency external charger and can easily attach to a backpack strap, pocket, or bill of a cap thanks to a two-way clip. On top of all of that, this thing is completely dustproof and waterproof up to 2 meters. —WB.

I tend to be pretty picky when it comes to outdoor and hiking hats. A lot of them look dorky, use cheap materials, or aren’t comfortable when you wear them. That’s why I was so stoked to find Fractel—a running hat company from Australia that blows most American outdoor hats away. The T-SIERPINKSKI Trucker Hats are stylish, lightweight, breathe well, and come in some wild colorways.—WB.

It has been revealed that leave it to Hyperlite to launch a product I didn’t know I needed, can’t really afford, and desperately want right before the holidays. The brand, known for its ultralight packs and shelters, relaunched its apparel line in 2026, and in November dropped an anorak made with waterproof 3-layer Dyneema. It weighs just 7.5 ounces. Do I need a upcoming anorak? Absolutely not. Would I love to keep this sweet little number in my backpacking kit? You bet. —WB.

I’m not usually the kind of hiker who’s willing to give up a hip belt on my pack, but the Volpi FastPack 30 was so much fun to use, it made me want to bring less stuff just so I could justify using it. The vest-style carry on this frameless model was comfortable, and stretch storage pockets on the straps and at the bottom (for a rain shell), plus a strap on top for carrying my sleeping pad, made organization simple. —Adam Roy, Editor-in-Chief.

According to recent reports, if I have a superpower, it’s being able to sleep anywhere, under any circumstances. Why not take advantage of that? I wouldn’t call Gossamer Gear’s Thinlight pads comfortable—at an eighth of an inch thick, they barely qualify as pads at all—but at just 2.7 ounces, they put even most cut-down closed-cell foam pads to shame when it comes to weight. —AR.

There’s a lot to like about the Soto Windmaster, which our testers picked out as the best backpacking stove of 2026. At just 3.1 ounces, it’s featherweight, and it performs consistently in the worst conditions, putting out a reliable flame without chewing through its gas supply even when it gets breezy. Thanks to its regulated design, it’s a solid pick for winter camping, too—a situation where some of my lightweight canister stoves have struggled. —AR.

It has been revealed that I’ve used a wide variety of inflatable craft during my time at Backpacker, from paddleboards to canoes. But few have impressed me as much as Alpacka’s Chinook, which tracked steadily and sliced through the water on an early-summer trip through Ruby Horsethief Canyon on the Colorado River. With its prominent bow and stern and removable skeg, the Chinook has some kayak DNA in its design, and paddles more like one than some of the squirrelly packrafts I’ve used. At 9.1 pounds, it’s light enough to haul, and in-tube storage and a clip-in point for a deck bag give it enough capacity for deep backcountry expeditions. —AR.

After more than a decade of use, my trusty lightweight tent from Brooks Range Mountaineering (RIP) is about to give up the ghost. (The manufacturer closed in 2018, if that tells you anything about how long I’ve been using it.) In my search for a replacement, I got to test out an X-Dome this fall, and I now see what all the fuss is about. This tent has a cult following for a reason: It’s featherweight at 44 ounces but doesn’t skimp on livability; the tall ceiling feels like a luxury for sitting up and changing inside. A simple pitch and details like the large doorways and generous internal pockets put this at the top of my list. —Zoe Gates, Senior Editor.

In a recent development, food is my love language and there’s nothing better than a consumable gift. I evangelize Stowaway Gourmet freeze dried meals to my backpacking friends any chance I get, because they are just so darn tasty. Perfect for a stocking stuffer, or spring for a 72-meal variety pack to feed your favorite hiker for a year. My faves: Drunken Noodles, Kimchi Jigae, Wild Boar Bacon Stew, and Cereal Killer. —ZG.

In a recent development, the time has come: After years on the trail, I am finally over inflating my sleeping pad manually. Over the years, I’ve tried all the methods, from lung power to foot pumps to inflation sacks. I’m ready to take one dreaded camp chore off my plate. A pad inflator is the height of luxury, and I can’t wait to indulge. —ZG.

It has been revealed that if someone really wants to spoil me this year, they’ll invest in a hobby I’ve always wanted to try: freeze drying my own backpacking meals. A dehydrator is an affordable gateway to the world of homemade trail meals, but freeze dryers (larger, more expensive) open up a whole latest world of food preservation. Freeze dried meals last longer than dehydrated ones, and maintain better texture and nutritional value—not to mention the wider range of ingredients that hold up to freeze drying. Armed with this appliance, I can spend my whole winter prepping meals for summer backpacking trips—and create some stocking stuffers of my own for the next holiday season. —ZG.

  • According to recent reports, gary Colliver passed away on August 30, 2026, in Denver, Colorado.
  • Recent findings suggest that throughout his life, Yosemite’s beauty was a current which drew him back, time and time again.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gary Colliver on 'Lucky Streaks' (5.10+), a six-pitch trad climb on Fairview Dome in Yosemite, in 1980. (Photo: Courtesy of Dave Sessions).

According to recent reports, gary Colliver passed away on August 30, 2026, in Denver, Colorado. He was 83. A longtime Yosemite Valley resident, he spent decades caring for the park as a ranger, medic, rescuer, and advocate.

Recent findings suggest that throughout his life, Yosemite’s beauty was a current which drew him back, time and time again. Colliver discovered climbing in college and soon moved to Camp 4. He met his future wife, Reva, in Tuolumne Meadows, married her in the Yosemite Valley Chapel in 1965, and built a decades-long career serving the park and its visitors.

In the early days of climbing in the Valley, Colliver was a quiet giant. With Richard McCracken and John Evans, he made the fourth ascent of the Nose (5.9 C2; 3,000ft) on El Capitan. He later returned to the route for the film El Capitan (1978), and in 1969, he climbed the Salathé Wall (5.9 C2; 3,500ft) with Chris Jones.

Later, his ambitions also took him beyond Yosemite. In 1964, he and Glen Denny made the first ascent of Jirishanca Norte (19,735ft) in Peru. In 1970, he joined Jones, Bob Cuthbert, and Gray Thompson for the first complete ascent of Mount Adamant’s north ridge in British Columbia. The following year, he participated in the International Himalayan Expedition to Mount Everest, where his team attempted a new route on Everest’s Southwest Face.

Industry observers note that to Dave Sessions, Colliver’s second cousin, those accomplishments belonged to an exceptionally modest man. “He was one of the most modest people I ever met in my life. Incredibly soft-spoken,” Sessions mentioned. “Never, never sought out attention or, you know, just very kind-hearted and modest and soft-spoken.”.

Industry observers note that colliver’s work in Yosemite included serving as a wilderness and climbing ranger, park medic, and volunteer firefighter. In 1983, he and two fellow rangers received a Department of the Interior Valor Award for rescuing a visitor from swift water.

His National Park Service colleague Mark Finscher worked alongside him on an early effort to develop a climbing management plan for the Valley, bringing together interest groups with opposing views on access, bolting, and responsible climbing.

In a recent development, “There were some strong personalities in that group, and Gary did a good job of dealing with that,” Finscher noted. Although that initial strategy was never formally signed, Colliver continued working in park planning and compliance. Finscher remembered him as an ally in upholding wilderness protections. “He never took the easy way,” he said.

Recent findings suggest that as a teenager, Sessions had asked Colliver whether he had been scared climbing El Capitan. He answered simply, “No, it was just so beautiful.” But for Colliver, the joy of being in Yosemite extended beyond any particular significant wall. “If he was in Yosemite, he was happy,” Sessions said.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Frankfurt, Germany (Photo: Lufthansa).

According to recent reports, nearly everybody visits Europe in summer. That’s no exaggeration: Half of all international inbound arrivals to the continent happen between June and September, with hotels, trails, attractions, and city streets swelling with nearly three times the people you’d encounter in January.

It has been revealed that that’s good news for winter fans. Seasonal highlights like festivals and craft markets and storybook scenery give winter travelers a whole different world to discover. Thanks to Lufthansa’s daily flights to its German city hubs from 18 U.S. cities coast to coast, enjoying the holiday traditions and empty museums requires very little effort. Just say yes.

Here’s how to get started on planning your winter getaway.

Frankfurt’s winter markets are best enjoyed on foot, as you’ll wind through more than 230 stalls. Fuel up for the walk with a Bethmännchen, the city’s traditional marzipan pastry, and warm up with a mug of hot apple wine before tracing your way along the Main River. Explore the famous Palmengarten glasshouses for a botanical escape to tropical, desert, and alpine environments, all within the urban core. Beyond the city, enjoy winter silence and peace on hundreds of marked winter trails crisscrossing the snow-dusted Taunus woods.

According to recent reports, see why this iconic city deserves its reputation as the international capital for modern culture. Stroll from the treed paths of the Tiergarten to Berlin’s many bridges (more than Venice). Sculptors and architects have turned all of Berlin into an open-air museum, but when the weather turns, you can duck into the galleries peppering the Auguststraße and Potsdamer Straße. Stay fueled at neighborhood cafés inspired by international cuisines, and join the late-night reveling at concerts and dance clubs. (Fresh Year’s Eve is a can’t-miss holiday.).

It has been revealed that elsewhere in Europe, there’s more to love about winter. In Italy, explore the eye-popping Dolomites, or visit Renaissance landmarks in Florence without the crowds. If you time it right, experience Venice’s Carnevale in late January and early February. In France, the Champs-Élysées Christmas market ends its decade-long absence this season, bringing 200 chalets to the famous Paris avenue. Prefer a warmer winter break? Head to Greece, where you can have Athens—and its ancient historic sites—practically to yourself. That’s easy to say yes to.

Whether you want to explore holiday magic in Germany, visit landmarks in Italy, or enjoy a warmer winter in Greece, Lufthansa gets you there.

The Lufthansa Group is a global aviation group with over 100,000 employees from 164 nations. In 2025, it carried more than 135 million passengers and generated €39.6 billion in revenue. Its largest segment, Passenger Airlines, includes the core airline Lufthansa and other leading European carriers, complemented by Logistics, MRO, IT, and Lufthansa Aviation Training.
