#90631. How I Sent ‘The Prophet’ and ‘Free Rider’ on El Cap in 18.5 Hours

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2368 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

How I Sent ‘The Prophet’ and ‘Free Rider’ on El Cap in 18.5 Hours

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2368 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that left to right: Alex Honnold, Connor Herson, and Tommy Caldwell take a celebratory selfie at the top of 'The Prophet' on El Cap.
  • It has been revealed that my alarm goes off, but I’m already wide awake; I never sleep well before an early start.
  • It has been revealed that established by Leo Houlding and Jason Pickles over a 10-year saga, The Prophet (5.13d/5.14a R; 1,800ft) has developed a reputation as one of El Cap’s scariest and most dangerous free routes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that left to right: Alex Honnold, Connor Herson, and Tommy Caldwell take a celebratory selfie at the top of 'The Prophet' on El Cap. (Photo: Courtesy of Alex Honnold).

It has been revealed that my alarm goes off, but I’m already wide awake; I never sleep well before an early start. I’ve got half an hour to pull myself together before Alex gets here and we start hiking. As I choke down breakfast, I can’t help but wonder if I’m in over my head. Despite Alex and Tommy’s best reassurances, The Prophet scares me.

It has been revealed that established by Leo Houlding and Jason Pickles over a 10-year saga, The Prophet (5.13d/5.14a R; 1,800ft) has developed a reputation as one of El Cap’s scariest and most dangerous free routes. Indeed, it’s broken a few bones over the years, and to this day, Leo and Jason’s ground up attempt remains one of the boldest and most heroic chapters in El Cap’s history. Growing up, I always told myself that I’d never climb The Prophet. Maybe I’d rap into the A1 Beauty (the splitter crux pitch, rated 5.13d, though Leo, Sonnie Trotter, and Alex have all talked of upgrading it to 5.14a1) to try it, but the rest of the route was too dangerous for me—I don’t do dangerous stuff.

Sources indicate that I wasn’t particularly surprised when Alex Honnold and Tommy Caldwell started trying The Prophet this season, but I watched their progress as a friend and spectator, not a potential suitor for the route. My own project on Leaning Tower was taking all my time this season.

On November 11, while eating breakfast and preparing for a day on my project, I ran into Alex and congratulated him on his send. He was hiking up that afternoon to belay Tommy, who was four days into his send push and trying the A1 Beauty. Alex offered to jumar and belay me on a ground-up push the next day, promising that the route was safer with his beta. I joked that I’d take him up if I couldn’t find a partner the next day for my project.

Recent findings suggest that I had a very promising session on my project, but that afternoon, I was still partnerless for the following day, so I called up Alex to ask if his offer was still valid. In between Tommy’s redpoint goes on the A1, Alex called me back to tell me what gear I’d need. We planned to start climbing around 4:00 a.m. the following morning.

Packing up that evening, I felt wholly unprepared. I’d been sport climbing all summer and hadn’t done more than about six pitches in a day since spring. The only valley granite I’d touched this season was my overhanging, physical project on Leaning Tower, which was almost certainly a different style from the slabby, polished, and technical El Cap granite ahead of me. I’d need to re-adapt efficiently and quickly, working with a lower stamina threshold than I was used to.

Hiking up the following morning on November 12, Alex started breaking down the route for me. He told me how he and Tommy had cleaned all the pitches, how they ticked and recorded every gear placement. As I started leading the first few pitches, I realized just how helpful this was going to be: I took only the exact rack I’d need for each pitch, and I didn’t have to stress at all about beta or gear. I took Alex at his word about the relative safety of each section (a risky decision, I know…) and tried to turn my brain off to the fullest extent possible.

Industry observers note that I settled into a sort of flow state; with the darkness obscuring any large runouts and Alex reassuring me of each gear placement ahead of me, I climbed calmly and intentionally over the lower pitches of the route. I couldn’t fathom Leo and Jason coming up here to find loose rock, grass-filled cracks, and no obvious route. It was certainly a far cry from my own experience on the freshly cleaned and ticked route. I remained relatively calm even over pitches four through six, the first few 5.13 pitches.

As we climbed higher and dawn broke, we saw Tommy above us; he’d not quite sent the night before, but he’d decided to spend another night on the wall and watch my attempt in the morning. With Tommy’s encouragement, I climbed the Guillotine Pitch (pitch eight, 5.13b), then the Devil’s Reacharound (pitch nine, 5.13a). Before long, I joined him at his portaledge at the base of the A1 Beauty just as the morning sun hit. What a perfect splitter it looked like, too—everything I could ever want in a pitch, at the very top of El Cap.

Recent findings suggest that the A1 Beauty sees direct sun from first light until sunset, and it bakes. It was already quite warm, and I figured it would only get warmer as the day progressed. Without much waiting, I racked up and started what I thought would be a beta sussing mission. A few moves in, I realized this attempt could be more than just that; with Tommy hanging on a static rope above me, telling me exactly what to do, I found myself through the low crux (~V8), then through the next section. As I got higher and higher, I tried to push down the feeling that I might just pull it off on this first attempt and instead focus on each move, each foothold, each gear placement. It felt perfect. Before I knew it, I was at the next anchor, absolutely thrilled.

Recent findings suggest that as excited as I was about the A1, suddenly the route became much more intense. I was only two pitches below the summit. Two pitches from flashing the entire route in a day. Two pitches from an El Cap flash. The following pitch was easy enough, but the exit pitch intimidated me: a 13b boulder problem right off the belay, involving an insecure standup on poor footholds.

Industry observers note that I climbed up to the boulder and back down to the belay a few times, feeling increasingly nervous. Eventually, I went for it: I placed the foot, took a deep breath, and stood. The foot held, and I excitedly reached for the next hold, which guards easier climbing to the top. I briefly lost focus, allowing a small voice to say, I’m doing it! It’s happening! The next thing I knew, my foot had slipped and I was hanging on the rope. My flash go was botched.

At that moment, I lost all perspective of the incredible morning of climbing I’d had; I was devastated. Half an hour later, topping out The Prophet after successfully climbing the pitch, I felt the most hollow I’ve felt upon topping out El Cap. Alex and Tommy joined me on top. As they packed their haulbag and portaledge, I couldn’t help but regret my missed opportunity.

According to recent reports, within a few minutes, however, I regained some perspective. It had been an incredibly memorable morning of climbing, and I’d still freed The Prophet ground-up in about seven hours. Only that morning, doing this would have been a dream come true, and I smiled a bit. I checked the time: 11:30 a.m. “Wow! I can drive home and meet my family in time for dinner!” I laughed and joked to Tommy and Alex.

Alex turned and gave me a wry smile. “You know, you could do a Double right now. Compared to The Prophet, Free Rider will probably feel pretty easy.”.

Tommy pitched in: “Yeah, I’d jug Free Rider this afternoon if you want!”.

Recent findings suggest that I stopped sorting my gear and stared. Great. I’m getting peer pressured by my heroes.

Industry observers note that among the rules I live by is that if Alex or Tommy offers something, I don’t turn them down. Especially a support mission on El Cap. As tired and emotionally drained as I was, I reminded myself just how much I’ve wanted to do the El Cap Double my entire life. I remembered topping out the free Nose-in-a-day last year, when I called every climber in the Valley to see if I could find a partner for a Double that day, to no avail. This sort of opportunity doesn’t come around particularly often. Even as I waffled about whether to go for it, the decision had been made. In a few hours’ time, I knew I’d be starting up Freeblast.

The climbing on Free Rider is significantly easier than on The Prophet, and I’d done most of the pitches when I freed the Salathé in 2022. I knew there would be little suspense about whether I’d be physically capable of sending it. However, I also knew I wasn’t in massive walling shape, and besides, this would be far and away the most pitches I’ve climbed in a day. I remember watching the video of Tommy freeing the El Cap double back in 2005, where he nearly lost it at the Enduro Corner. I wondered if I was in for a similar bout.

The first few pitches on Free Rider went remarkably smoothly. Alex, still keen on supporting me, had jugged our day pack up the Heart Lines, which made Freeblast an absolute breeze. My feet were hurting, but I could feel the ibuprofen I’d pounded at the base starting to kick in. I settled into a flow, and pitch after pitch flew past. I felt remarkably fresh. With Tommy’s encouragement and psych, I was optimistic.

Industry observers note that around the Monster Offwidth (pitch 20 of 30 on Free Rider), darkness fell. I could feel the fatigue building; our pace slowed, but we kept moving. I was making a conscious effort to stay positive and cheerful, to act like I had endless energy in the hopes that I could fake that energy into existence.

In a recent development, when we reached the crux, I opted for the Teflon Corner instead of the Boulder Problem. I’d never tried the Boulder before, and I didn’t want my first attempt to be 40-odd pitches into the day. The Teflon went down on my first try, and before long, we were at the Enduro Corner. Tommy suggested that I skip the hanging belay at the end of the Enduro Corner and link it into the Round Table Traverse. I rolled my eyes, thinking that I’d be lucky to scrape my way up the Corner on its own, but to my surprise, I felt remarkably fresh. I reached the hanging belay and kept climbing, thankful to have cleared that last hurdle.

At 10:45 p.m., a little more than eight hours after starting Free Rider and 18.5 hours after starting up The Prophet, Tommy and I topped out to strong, cold winds. We didn’t stick around long to celebrate; already shivering, we swiftly packed and started running to stay warm on the hike down. As we got lower and warmed up, however, we slowed down and soaked in the unforgettable day we’d just had: around 45 pitches of climbing for a free El Cap Double!

Sources indicate that alex and Tommy both have families. They both had good reason to rush home ahead of the incoming storm instead of supporting some kid who wanted to try their project. And to be honest, I wouldn’t have blamed them if they didn’t want me to mooch off their hard work prepping The Prophet. There’s absolutely no way I could have done The Prophet ground up and in a day without the labor Tommy and Alex spent to find the route, clean loose rock, and find all the gear beta. After four days on the wall and away from his family, I would have completely understood if Tommy wanted to get home to his kids rather than go up El Cap a second time that day—especially with Tioga Pass imminently closing, which meant supporting me on Free Rider would lengthen his drive home by about an hour.

Recent findings suggest that nevertheless, their support that day exemplifies the exact values I love to see in climbing. This is the sport I want climbing to be: one where the giants, the biggest legends of the game, are generous enough to go out of their way to help younger up-and-comers. A sport where the younger generation is not seen as a fresh wave of competition but is instead embraced and mentored.

Not flashing The Prophet is certainly going to sting for a while. I still replay that moment on the exit pitch daily, and I’m sure I’ll always feel some regret about it. Still, the more I reflect on that day, the more Alex and Tommy’s support stands out to me. Every outing leaves us with a lesson or slightly shifted worldview. In 10 or 20 years, I’m confident that looking back on the El Cap Double will remind me that there is a world larger than my own climbing; that, like Tommy and Alex, I can make another climber’s entire season by simply offering them a few hours of my time and a bit of encouragement. As I grow and find my place in the climbing world, I can only hope to be as influential a mentor to future generations.

In a recent development, the 10,000-BTU Zempire Stealth Jet Twin isn’t the most powerful camp stove we’ve ever tested, but it is the slimmest two-burner we’ve ever tested, making it a sweet gift for car campers who value trunk space and camp cuisine alike. Easy simmer controls and built-in igniters round this pick out as a major upgrade for campers still lugging WWII-era camp stoves that weigh as much as small sedans.

Recent findings suggest that both a firepit and a grill, Snow Peak’s Takibi is designed to be the centerpiece of camp life. While it’s a delight just to watch flames flicker in the portable stainless steel pit, the well-crafted, Japanese-made Takibi is an excellent charcoal grill. Pair it with Snow Peak camp cooking accessories to help your loved one build out the ultimate live-fire cooking setup.

Sources indicate that we love the versatility of the Switch. It comes with an integrated pot for fast boiling à la Jetboil, but remove the pot and the prongs unfurl like those on a classic canister stove to accommodate bigger pots and pans. For backpackers who like to cook—but appreciate the convenience of dehydrated meals from time to time—the Switch is a nifty, thoughtful gift.

When backpackers want to cut down on pack weight, they often opt for titanium cookware and accessories, as the metal offers an unbeatable strength-to-weight ratio. No one does titanium quite like Snow Peak. Smaller pieces, like Snow Peak’s iconic sporks, are a backpacker’s dream stocking stuffer, while drinkware and cooksets are destined to become prized possessions.

The compact and efficient Campstove 2+ can boil one liter of water in four and a half minutes, so it has morning coffee covered (you can also cook on it with some add-on components).

This isn’t your usual camping stove, though. It runs on biofuel—either pellets you can purchase or sticks you find. And this stove has multiple uses: It can also charge your devices via an integrated USB port as well as function as a lamp with its included attachment.

According to recent reports, rare is the pan that can handle an open flame, an induction cooktop, and a piping-hot pizza oven. Adaptable, durable, and dependable, this pan is ready for adventurous weekends at camp and cozy weeknights at home.

In a recent development, quince’s Hinoki Cutting Boards make ditching the microplastic-shedding chopping blocks of yesteryear a genuine pleasure. The wood is also naturally lightweight, making it easy to pack these boards into your camp kitchen bin.

Socks are always a slam-dunk stocking stuffer. Fun, hilarious, nostalgic, and comfortable to boot, these cotton crew socks are sure to earn a grin every time they’re dug out of the sock drawer. What more can we say but… BAM!

You might be wondering what the hell is Outside doing writing about a KitchenAid Tilt-Head Stand Mixer? It’s a fair question. The truth is that we’re major fans of baked goods around here. Whether we’re exploring via skintrack or singletrack, a well-timed lemon bar or squished chocolate chip muffin can make all the difference. And besides, the forest-green colorway and the natural woodgrain bowl make this mixer quite a thoughtful gift for the nature-loving baker, no? It’s on our holiday wish list, at least!

Industry observers note that being landlocked is no longer a problem for seafood-loving gourmands. Industry observers note that whether we’re cooking at home or at camp, the first ingredient we reach for is usually olive oil. A sampler set lets you gift multiple options—and the brand’s spice selection isn’t bad either.

In a recent development, some people say their love language is touch. Others say acts of service. For some, it’s caffeine, delivered shortly after waking, preferably in bed. If a caffeine addict is on your list, Equator Coffee, a longtime California roaster, offers curated coffee subscriptions that speak that love language fluently. Oh—and its instant coffee is an epic stocking stuffer for backpackers who can’t hit the trail without some jet fuel.

There are a million gizmos and gadgets out there for the espresso fanatics, the drip disciples, the press-and-plunge crowd. But what about the nitro lovers? Behold: the Cumulus Coffee Machine. An all-in-one robot for chilled coffee lovers that brings barista-grade bevies into the comfort of your own home, the machine has three settings that allow you to convert Cumulus pods into iced espresso, crisp cold brew, and creamy nitro. The nitro setting is particularly rad, as the Cumulus sources nitrogen from ambient air—no nitrogen cartridges required. And there’s no ice required, either, as the machine self-chills. This is a dream gift for any cold brew connoisseur, but especially those who order nitro on the regular.

How My First Multi-Pitch Climb Became a Midnight Barefoot Epic

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1346 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, on July 4, 2026, Audrey Callaway climbed her first real multi-pitch: Diedre (5.8, 6 pitches) in Squamish, B.C.
  • After first getting into the sport at a gym in Chicago, Callaway later moved to upstate New York near the Gunks.
  • Callaway wanted to share her experience to highlight the growing pains of “doing things poorly the first time”—and how the right partners ease those pains.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, on July 4, 2026, Audrey Callaway climbed her first real multi-pitch: Diedre (5.8, 6 pitches) in Squamish, B.C. The catch? She didn’t start up pitch one until nearly 9 p.m., thus becoming voluntarily benighted in only the most literal sense of the term. “My story isn’t a disaster!” Callaway explains. “It’s about learning, the tenacity of a little psych, and extremely good manufacturer.”.

After first getting into the sport at a gym in Chicago, Callaway later moved to upstate New York near the Gunks. At the moment, she’s studying forestry at the University of Vermont. “I like trees, I like climbing, I like birds,” she claims of her substantial three hobbies. She’s mostly a boulderer and sport climber who wants to get more into trad climbing. She also works at a climbing gym.

Callaway wanted to share her experience to highlight the growing pains of “doing things poorly the first time”—and how the right partners ease those pains. Below, she shares her story and what others embarking on their first multi-pitch can learn from her experience.

It’s really cool to feel very bad at something again.

I was planning to visit my girlfriend Lucy, who had been in Squamish for the whole summer. Then my best friend Will, who I grew up climbing with at the gym, told me he also happened to be going out to Squamish. I got there a few days before him and did a little bouldering.

Industry observers note that when Will got there, he was even more psyched than I was. After bouldering all afternoon, we’re sitting around, playing chess and looking through Lucy’s guidebook when we saw a trad climb that looked so cool: Diedre (5.8, 6 pitches).

Sources indicate that it was 7 p.m., but the sun didn’t set until around 9 p.m. It was very spur of the moment. We’re just like, “We gotta do this thing.” So we promptly got all our stuff together.

In a recent development, we knew it was going to get dark. It’s not like it snuck up on us. But Lucy had a lot of experience. Will and I didn’t know how to trad climb at this point, although he learned later on that trip. So she’s carrying the team. Afterward, she told me she brought only a single rack so that she could share in our sense of adventure and “empathize with the uncertainty.”.

It has been revealed that first, we got super lost on the way there. We didn’t get to the base of the climb until like 8:45 p.m., but it was still super bright out.

It has been revealed that very rapidly, I realized how bad I was at rope management. I was in the middle, belaying Lucy, and we had two ropes. Routefinding is something that you take for granted when you’ve been climbing outside for a while. I was taking the path of most resistance. There was a pretty solid crack on really good terrain, but I’m newer to crack climbing, so I was not about to put my hands in there and trust that. Instead, I was doing this very sketchy 5.10 slab. Eventually, I started using the crack.

It has been revealed that we got up to the first belay and we’re all on top of each other because we don’t really know where to be. Nothing was unsafe, but it was very slow. Lucy started going up this 5.6 very runout slab. But I had looped a knot of rope around where I was belaying. I didn’t realize that until I’d fed out enough of the slack. So I kept shorting her like every five feet. I knew that there was totally a way to fix this, but I don’t know how.

In a recent development, then the sun set. That’s okay, because we had headlamps—but Lucy’s headlamp was dead. It was funny because before we started climbing, Lucy was like, “Guys, make sure you have your headlamps.” But then when we put them on, she’s like, “Can I actually borrow yours?”.

It has been revealed that so she took mine, and now I was climbing in the dark on slab. It was very precarious, but beautiful. It felt so scary in the moment. But the town was right there, we’re on the most classic 5.8 ever, and we’re a hundred feet off the ground—it wasn’t actually that scary.

Industry observers note that will and I both had super competitive shoes on. It had been two hours at this point and we’re standing on this slab and our feet were killing us. Every time I left the belay, Will told me he “would lowkey start crying a bit” because he knew he’d have to climb soon, enduring more toe pain. So we both took off our shoes because it’s easier to climb barefoot. Now I was barefoot in the dark on this slab.

Every time we got to a newly introduced belay, we tried to make the system better. Lucy was just trying to climb, but we’re shorting her every time. Now Will was in the way. We were right on top of each other.

None of these things were particularly hard challenges. If we knew what we were doing, we could have fixed any one of these problems in 30 seconds. I would get back up to Lucy and she would be like, “Why didn’t you just do this?” Then something else would come up.

At one point, probably around 11:30 p.m., Will got a cam stuck. Lucy’s like, “Try wiggling it.” She told him to pull upward, but he mentioned it was literally impossible. Lucy lowered down and pulled it out, first try. There must have been times like this when Lucy was frustrated, but she never showed it. Will describes Lucy as the most patient person he’s ever met.

We got to the top at midnight. It was hypnotizing on the apron. The lights of town beneath us glowed surreally. I smoked my first cigarette at the top.

Industry observers note that I remember walking back and it was really quiet. We got back on the road and our gear’s rattling and the moon’s out. It was so quiet and peaceful.

It has been revealed that it was one in the morning when we got back to the campground by the Chief. We didn’t want to be disrespectful with a significant light, so we put a headlamp under this pickle jar we had. By the light of this pickle lamp, we ate pickles and cold canned minestrone and asked, “What are we gonna do tomorrow?”.

To really be benighted, I would say it has to sneak up on you. It kinda felt like it snuck up on me. Clearly, as a group we were aware it was about to happen. But I was surprised when all of a sudden it was dark and I had no headlamp and was climbing barefoot. It made me feel like a salamander, really in touch with the rock.

Lucy and I did another multi-pitch the next day, and since then I’ve done a couple two-pitch climbs in the Gunks when I got back to Newly introduced York. I will probably do lots of really awesome multi-pitches in my lifetime that are beautiful and scenic with really hard climbing, but I’m never gonna have another one that bad. I’m never gonna have another first one.

Sources indicate that as told to Maya Silver. This story has been edited for length, structure, and clarity.

Your kids might not remember what was under the tree, but we promise they’ll never forget the nights spent under the stars with their family. Lucky for parents, outdoor gear is more family-friendly than ever. Think: tents you can stand up in, paddle boards that pack into a backpack, campsite games, passenger-friendly e-bikes, and so much more. These 12 adventure-ready gifts are for the families on your list who’d rather spend the weekend at the campsite, on the water, or on the bike path than on the couch with an iPad in hand.

Recent findings suggest that the best part of birding is that there’s no real age requirement or limit. It’s arguably one of the most accessible (and relaxing) ways for families to enjoy the outdoors. Everyone from toddlers to grandparents can find joy in spotting bird species with these lightweight binoculars. Heck, you can get the grandparents out there, too! Psst…we have lots more birding gear recs where this came from.

You don’t have to give up hiking if you’ve got little ones. It just takes some helpful gear to keep the adventure going strong. Add a hiking backpack carrier to your gear closet so it’s easy to get your kids on the trail. Backpack carriers are best for youngins under 5 years old or 55 pounds. Our favorite pick for longer hiking trails is the Deuter Kid Comfort Child Carrier, which fits like a backpacking pack and includes tons of features to make hiking with kids much easier. And if you’re lucky, you just might squeeze some trail naps in.

Camp games, anyone? ENO’s latest TrailFlyer game is like bags (or cornhole, as we call it in the Midwest) but designed for camping. It packs down into a small carrying case and takes just a few minutes to set up. Wrap the adjustable straps around a tree trunk or sturdy anchor point, stake out the feet, and start tossing.

According to recent reports, our family has put the heavy-duty Victory Patio Blanket to use as a play area for our crawling baby at camp, and we’ve taken it to plenty of beach days and park picnics. The underside is coated in a thick, waterproof material that keeps moisture and dirt from seeping through. You can also toss it in your tent to make a cozier floor or dress up your campsite with an outdoor rug.

Recent findings suggest that good luck wrapping a kayak (or fitting it in your garage). Skip the bulky gift for the packable and portable inflatable ISLE Switch 3. This hybrid SUP-kayak fits in a backpack with everything you need to hit the water, including a paddle, pump, and inflatable kayak seats. It’s the perfect adventure gift for a family who loves getting out on the water.

It has been revealed that keep it old school with this point-and-shoot camera that’s perfectly nostalgic. Don’t let its lack of a screen fool you. This screen-free digital camera is rechargeable and can capture up to 500 photos per charge. It also offers several built-in filters—standard, vintage, analog, and black-and-white—that you can swap with the push of a button. Bonus: it comes with a microSD card already inside, so you’ve got room for around 2,000 photos from day one.

It has been revealed that if you want to take the littlest adventures with all their gear along, this wagon makes it easy. It works three ways: as a wagon for hauling, as a stroller with two 5-point safety harness seats, and as a car seat carrier with the included adapter (car seat not included).

Sources indicate that the Wrangler Deluxe holds up to 110 pounds and brings the tough, trail-ready spirit Jeep is known for, with all-terrain puncture-proof airless tires and swivel front wheels for easy maneuvering. A removable cooler bag holds up to 16 cans, and the wagon also has a UV-blocking canopy, pull-down shades, a cup holder, a parent organizer, and multiple storage pockets. When it’s time to pack up, it folds compactly.

Cozy up around the campfire with the ones you love in this two-seater camp chair. Its low-profile, reclined design puts you at just the right height for roasting s’mores and soaking up the fire’s warmth. And for a chair that fits two (or three if you’ve got a kiddo on your lap), it packs down surprisingly small.

We can’t mention s’mores without plugging our favorite roasting sticks. These reusable, telescoping metal roasting forks make great stocking stuffers. Our set has lasted through years of camping, and we love using them not only for marshmallows but also for hot dogs, sausages, and the occasional Twinkie.

Due for a new family cooler? Keep beers, bubbly water, juice boxes, and everything in between ice-cold in the Hydro Flask 15L Carryout Soft Cooler. It’s easy to carry and easy to clean, which makes it a go-to for camping trips, road trips, soccer tournaments, and backyard grill-outs. Don’t worry about scratches, broken buckles, or dings, either: Hydro Flask offers a lifetime warranty.

According to recent reports, who needs a minivan when you’ve got the Aventon Abound LR? This cargo e-bike is made for family adventures in the city and beyond, featuring an extra-long rear rack that fits two kids (or one kiddo plus panniers full of gear). Hills are no match for its powerful 750W motor, and you can ride up to 60 miles on a single charge. We opted for the smaller Abound SR since we’re a “one-and-done” family, but the LR is a great upgrade if you have more kids and gear to haul.

Sources indicate that give the gift of camping! Hipcamp takes the stress out of snagging a campsite before it sells out. Its database of private land available for rent connects you with one-of-a-kind stays—from tent sites on farms and vineyards to cabins, glamping tents, and treehouses. All you have to do is dream up your family’s perfect night under the stars.

The perfect family camping tent doesn’t exis—oh wait, there’s The North Face Wawona 6. It’s tall enough to stand up in, sleeps six, features tons of interior pockets, and has color-coded poles to make setup a breeze. Speaking of a breeze, oversized mesh windows help ventilate the tent on muggy summer nights. The best part? A huge vestibule that works like a front porch, giving you a shady and dry spot to kick back in camp chairs in hot or rainy weather.

The Gozney Arc XL pizza oven makes outdoor entertaining easy year-round, from backyard pizza parties to après-ski gatherings. (Photo: Courtesy of Gozney).

Sources indicate that I wrote about my Gozney Arc XL pizza oven two summers ago, when it became the pie de resistance for using my backyard to get outside more (and for a suspicious number of latest friends showing up at my house). More than a year later, I’m happy to report that the novelty hasn’t worn off. If anything, I love it more.

Industry observers note that one of my favorite ways to spend a Sunday afternoon, or unwind after a mountain bike ride, is inviting friends over for homemade pizzas. Everyone brings their favorite toppings, we experiment with different combinations, and dinner becomes an activity in itself. It’s dinner and a show, and everyone gets fed. And because we keep ours on a covered porch with adequate ventilation, pizza night doesn’t end when winter arrives. Après-ski pizza parties might actually be my favorite use for it.

The Gozney Arc XL makes it ridiculously easy. It runs on propane (I use the same tank from my grill), reaches temperatures up to 950°F, and can cook a 16-inch pizza in as little as 60 seconds. Its lateral rolling flame distributes heat across the oven, so you don’t have to constantly rotate your pizza. The result is that perfectly blistered, chewy crust I usually associate with my favorite wood-fired pizza joints now in my own backyard.

Gozney makes several ovens, from more portable models to larger, more elaborate setups (many are also on sale right now). The Arc XL hits the sweet spot for me because it’s compact enough for our back patio, still with plenty of room to maneuver a full-size pizza.

You can make your own dough, buy Gozney’s mixes, or do what we do: keep Trader Joe’s premade pizza dough in the freezer so we’re always ready for an impromptu pizza night. One tip: a little semolina flour on your pizza peel helps the dough slide into the oven without sticking.

It has been revealed that my favorite toppings? Peaches, burrata, prosciutto, basil, and hot honey. Comment yours!

Industry observers note that learn from my mistake. When I first bought my Arc XL, I skipped the matching stand for a cheaper rolling cart from Amazon. It was a nightmare to assemble, felt flimsy, and looked terrible. I recently upgraded to the actual Gozney stand, and the difference is night and day. It’s sturdy, streamlined, easy to move, and designed to hold the oven securely. I should have trusted Gozney from the start.

Sources indicate that the stand has a 4.8-out-of-5-star rating from 204 customer reviews, so apparently plenty of people knew something I didn’t. Worth the upgrade, especially while it’s on sale.

If you’re shopping for someone who already owns a Gozney, the brand’s pizza peels, dough trays, and other accessories make excellent gifts and are also on sale for Black Friday.

Some people book a luxury hotel for the weekend. Others would rather throw a tent in the car and figure out where they’re sleeping later. If you have one of the latter on your holiday shopping list, we’ve got you covered. Below are the best camping gifts that will make their time outside a bit more comfortable—even if they swear they don’t care about that. From the practical gear they’ll use on every trip to the fun extras that let them have their creature comforts, these presents will have them plotting their getaway ASAP.

In a recent development, A good pair of hiking socks is always appreciated, but these come with a little extra feel-good factor. Made with 70 percent organic cotton and a cushioned footbed, Conscious Step socks are comfortable enough for long days on the trail (or lazy ones around camp). Even better, purchases support the National Parks Conservation Association, which works to protect America’s public lands.

This interactive water bottle doubles as an excuse to initiative their next big camping trip. It comes with 63 illustrated, water-resistant stickers representing every national park in the U.S., so they can track where they’ve visited as they go. Since it’s a Nalgene, it’s also durable and featherlight, perfect for hanging from backpacks and gear bags.

Industry observers note that this is the ideal gift for the person who considers coffee a nonnegotiable, regardless of how far they’ve wandered from civilization. This compact brewer is roughly the size of a thermos and makes hot coffee and cold brew concentrate in minutes. Simply add finely ground coffee and hot or cold water, let it brew, then use the hand press to dispense a concentrated shot into the included carafe. With no plugs and no charging required, they can throw it in their bag and go.

It has been revealed that camp chairs are great, but they’re not always the easiest things to lug around. This compact stool weighs just 1.2 pounds, folds down to 7.5 inches, and has a swiveling seat that lets you turn without having to pick up and reposition the whole thing. It supports up to 260 pounds, too, which is impressive for its size.

Sources indicate that this is a particularly useful piece of gear for any camper who wants to cut down on what they’re carrying. Hydrapak’s collapsible flask has a built-in filter that removes common waterborne bacteria and parasites, allowing hikers to refill from water sources along the trail. It weighs just 4.1 ounces and packs completely flat when empty. It’s a great option for biking, hiking, paddling, and even traveling through sketchy airport bathrooms.

A headlamp is one of those camping essentials you don’t fully appreciate until you’re stumbling around camp in the dark. The Storm delivers up to 550 lumens with adjustable brightness, three different colored modes (red, blue, and green) to preserve night vision, and a waterproof-rated IPX7 construction that can handle rain and snow. It also has a lock mode to prevent it from accidentally turning on in your pack and draining the batteries before you even reach camp.

It has been revealed that if you want your family and friends to experience comfort in camp, look no further than this hammock. The kit has everything someone needs to set up between two trees, including polyester straps and iron carabiners. The Portable Hammock has a weight capacity of 551 pounds and it exhibits both the toughness and user-friendliness that Jeep is known for: It’s made from durable nylon and conveniently packs away into a built-in pouch that doubles as a pocket when the hammock is set up.

It has been revealed that there are hundreds of camp slippers on the market, but few are as truly warm or versatile as Glerups. Made from 100 percent natural wool, they’re naturally temperature-regulating and odor-resistant, so feet stay comfortable without getting swampy. The slip-on design makes them easy to kick off tent-side, while the rubber sole handles dirt, mud, and slippery moss with ease.

Finicky sleepers will love this sleeping bag. The Kelty Eclipse skips the traditional zipper in favor of a clever wraparound design that campers spread out when they’re hot or cocoon themself when they’re cold. What it lacks in zippers it makes up for in thoughtful details, including a self-sealing foot vent, oversized hood to keep pillows in place, and internal pockets. It’s also rated to 15 degrees Fahrenheit, so it’s built for more than just balmy summer nights.

According to recent reports, A good outdoor blanket earns its keep in just about every situation, and Yeti’s Lowlands is designed to handle more than one night under the stars. Its waterproof, puncture-resistant bottom keeps damp ground from seeping through, while the cushioned top provides a comfortable place to sit, stretch out, or let the dog settle in. Roll it up for transport, then bring it out for everything from picnics to beach days to tailgates.

In a recent development, if their cooking kit is just a recycled takeout container and one random spork, please get them this Gerber set. The 16-piece set includes a saute pan, stock pot, hot pad, and tableware for four people, giving them everything they need to make and serve a proper meal without cobbling together a kitchen from mismatched gear. When they’re finished, everything nests together for easy packing until the next time they need it.

These are the pants they’ll put on once at camp and have absolutely no interest in taking off, especially in colder temps. The Fernos pair a cozy insulated interior with a water-resistant exterior, making them ideal for chilly mornings, lounging around the campsite, or layering over a base layer when snow starts to fall. In other words, they’re very durable sweatpants.

This is about as close as campers can get to bringing their mattress into the woods. The 3.9-inch memory foam pad is thick, supportive, and genuinely comfortable—more proper bed than half-deflated sleeping pad situation. It’s not designed for backpacking (don’t try to carry this on a thru-hike), but it’s portable enough to toss in the car for weekend camping trips. It rolls up tightly for storage and transport and self-inflates when unrolled, making set-up a breeze.

One of the best things about Luno’s car camping mattresses is that they’re not reserved for people with tricked-out 4x4s. The Air Pro is designed to fit a wide range of vehicles, with custom-fit options for dozens of makes and models. This particular kit includes a luxe inflatable mattress, air pump, fitted sheet, pillow, and window screen set that turns their backseat into a dreamy place to sleep. Simply put in their car’s year, make, and model and choose their window size for the gift of spontaneous overnights and long road trips.

This is for the camp chef who thinks camping dinner should involve way more than hot dogs and s’mores. The Gozney Tread is a portable pizza oven that heats up to 950°F and cooks a delicious pie in about a minute. Its compact design makes it shockingly easy to transport and it runs on propane, so they won’t need to fuss with building a fire. Sure, it’s a bit of a splurge for the campsite, but the lucky recipient will have no trouble convincing their camping buddies it’s worth the extra trunk space.

Industry observers note that all campers know that a tent you can properly stand up in is the gift that keeps on giving. The Aurora Highrise has near-vertical walls and a roomy interior that comfortably accommodates up to six people, making it a good pick for families or groups who don’t love sleeping elbow-to-elbow. Large windows and doors let in plenty of light and airflow, while Nightlight Pockets let headlamps and flashlights cast an ambient glow. There’s also a generous vestibule for stashing muddy boots, camping chairs, and anything else that needs protection overnight.

Edelrid manufactured this 70m rope with over 40% renewable materials, leveraging a bio-based polyamide in part made from castor oil. Interchangeable screw-on head weights let us dial in balance for any terrain, and the razor-thin picks—2.5 millimeters at the tip versus a 3- to 3.5-millimeter industry average—place like a dream. Read more about the Hydras in our Winter Gear Guide.

It has been revealed that our best all-around helmet of Fall 2026, the Black Diamond Vision offers the best of both worlds when it comes to comfort and weight. Made from mostly foam, with a plastic, ABS hardshell covering a portion of the top of the helmet, the Vision is impressively light at 215 grams.

They are easy to put on, simple to clip to a back gear loop of your harness (I keep them clipped under my chalkbag), comfortable, and super durable on sandstone, granite, and human-made cracks alike.

How to Crew an Ultramarathon Like a Pro

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2161 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission.
  • Addison Smith is an ultrarunning coach at CTS, one of the most popular and accomplished coaching organizations in endurance sports.
  • Crewing a runner at a trail race may seem like a simple task and, in a lot of ways, it is.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Addison Smith is an ultrarunning coach at CTS, one of the most popular and accomplished coaching organizations in endurance sports. He’s headed up the CTS team’s crewing logistics and efforts for races like the Western States 100 and Leadville 100 for years, helping athletes land multiple podium finishes, course records, and Golden Tickets.

Crewing a runner at a trail race may seem like a simple task and, in a lot of ways, it is. But in the thick of the moment, it can also be stressful, chaotic, and leave you feeling powerless in a situation you hadn’t prepared for. I’ve crewed at a wide variety of trail and ultra races for both cutoff chasers and elite athletes alike. For the past four years, I’ve led the Carmichael Training Systems (CTS) crewing operations for our team crewing efforts at the Western States 100, Javelina 100, Leadville 100, and Canyons Endurance Events. Each race has its own flavor of support, from the rules on the type of assistance you can give, to how frequently you can assist, and how many members each crew can have.

Industry observers note that ultrarunning really is a team sport, and the proficiency of the crew can be the difference between winning or losing, finishing or DNFing. I’ve seen crew talk a discouraged and fatigued but physically healthy athlete into quitting because they weren’t confident in how to help them through their low patch. I’ve also seen a well-treated blister and some words of encouragement get an athlete back on their pacing plan after a few miles of spiraled thoughts and painful steps.

The following is a framework for streamlining the crewing process. It’s less a gear guide on what’s in my blister kit and the type of power bank I like using, and more about preparing you to organize and ask the right questions so you can crew with confidence when your runner is depending on you.

Sources indicate that crewing is a selfless act of caring for a runner. But, paradoxically, it requires a deliberate effort of self-care by the members of the crew as well. For anyone who has crewed a race that lasts most of the day—if not multiple days—you know just how mentally and physically fatiguing an endeavor it can be. You may not be physically running the race, but you’re trying to juggle logistical details—often sleep deprived and outside in harsh conditions. With so many moving pieces, crew members often forget to drink or eat enough themselves—which can show up in the way they communicate or execute their role. Remember that, although some of the tips and tasks outlined below can be time-consuming, the additional organization will hopefully relieve stress, save time, and improve not only your availability for your athlete, but also your enjoyment of the crewing experience.

Crews of various sizes can be successful. In general, three people is ideal in most scenarios for efficiency and effectiveness. The first crew member can focus on restocking fuel, hydration, and equipment. The second crew member can focus on tending to the athlete directly. They will be the main communicator; giving advice and reassurance, while also tending to their immediate physical needs like cooling or blisters. The third crew member is the pacer. Their primary job is preparing themselves for the long stretch of miles they will run with the athlete by taking care of themselves throughout the day, resting, fueling, and saving energy before their run.

Recent findings suggest that specific races would certainly require more crew. For example, the Badwater 135 is a great example of a race where four crew members would be ideal. Crew vehicles are required to follow each athlete along the course, and crews are allowed to pace athletes after Stovepipe Wells (Mile 42). If two people are tasked with driving and pacing, having another crew member ready to cool the athlete and swap bottles every few miles keeps the frequent need for crewing in the hot temperatures efficient. Not to mention having a fourth crew member to fill in and take turns allows crew members to rest and stay fresh in a race that typically takes more than 35 hours to complete.

While three to four person crews are ideal, they may not be a possibility for some athletes. I know many couples who crew their significant other by themselves in 100 mile races—often to great success. If you find yourself in a single-person crew situation, most races have a multitude of helpful volunteers at aid stations that can assist you in crewing when needed. Three to four prepared crew members may give the best chance to be as efficient through an aid station as possible, but it certainly isn’t an absolute necessity for success.

I would define crewing as people meeting an athlete at aid stations during a race to give physical and emotional support to help them accomplish their race goals. The distinction between physical and emotional support provides the general framework I use to prepare to crew effectively. The physical support could be boiled down to efficient problem solving and transitions, and the emotional side of things to empowering interactions (or a psychological pick-me-up). As crew members, we have an opportunity to give physical support (fueling, hydration, gear, cooling, etc.), as well as emotional support (acknowledgement, guidance, tone, motivation, etc.). You can be incredibly organized as a crew, but if you give the wrong emotional support, it could affect your athlete’s race just as much—if not more—than not being prepared with the proper equipment or nutrition. You need to be prepared for both sides of the crewing process to give both yourself and your athlete the best experience possible.

Below, I’ll break down my guidelines to being both physically and emotionally supportive for your athlete.

Though this might seem like the most straightforward tip, it’s the one that requires the most planning beforehand. When crewing, you need to prepare  by having the right tools and gear for a variety of situations your athlete might find themselves in–whether that’s dealing with heat, high altitude, an upset stomach, blisters, heat, cold, or any number of other issues. Here’s a checklist of essential gear that CTS coaching uses at the majority of trail and ultra races we crew:.

It has been revealed that going into the race, it’s important to know how your athlete’s preparation went in the lead-up, what their goals are for the race, as well as their pacing, fueling, hydration, and gear strategies. Once the race starts, it’s equally important to collect real-time information via timing splits or from other crew members. This information gives you a clearer picture of how the race is going, and helps you anticipate what might be needed at the next crewing opportunity.

Industry observers note that below is what we refer to as an “athlete tracking card”. It is an easy-to-use document that summarizes the necessary context of crewing, so when it’s 2 a.m. and you can’t juggle all of the information needed, you’re still able to reorient yourself around the most vital details. Whether you’re a first time crew member or an experienced one, I strongly recommend creating your own version of this card to correctly orient yourself around the critical contextual information for the specific athlete and race demands.

According to recent reports, the last piece to successful physical crewing is effective communication between crew members. Sometimes crewing is a one-person job, but that usually isn’t the case. Ultras often require multiple people to handle various tasks like driving, pacing, cooling, nutrition, etc. The more you can delegate roles–and stick to those roles–the more efficient you can be getting an athlete in and out of the aid station. Once a role has been assigned within the group, it’s up to that person to own their role. In other words, each person should know what gear they need. For example, the person in charge of cooling should know where the bucket, water, and ice are. Each person should also take the initiative to ask the athlete ahead of time how they want the task performed. If you’re in charge of bottles, nutrition, or an athlete’s pack, you should know exactly where they want each item. Owning your role also allows for a more efficient and less stressful pivot if something goes awry.

In a recent development, in all of my experience at races watching athlete and crew scenarios play out, this is the aspect of crewing that is most easily mishandled. Let’s dive into a race scenario:.

It has been revealed that you’re racing the Leadville 100 and the second summit of Hope Pass is in your rearview mirror. You’ve been at 10,000 feet or more for most of the day, you’re tired, under-fueled, slightly dehydrated, and you’ve rallied through some stomach challenges. The sun is finally starting to go down and the temperatures are dropping. Your muscles ache and you’re starting to get a hot spot on your foot, but you’re still moving fairly well just behind your goal pace. You can’t wait to get to the Twin Lakes inbound aid station to see your crew, and you’re excited to pick up your pacer. When you get to the aid station, your crew waves you into your tent. You tell them you haven’t been able to get food down consistently, you’re developing hot spots, you don’t want to take in gels anymore, and the planned electrolyte mix sounds terrible now. You ask what you should try. The crew turns to each other, perplexed, saying, “This wasn’t in the plan, what do we do now?” For the next five minutes, the crew peppers you with a dozen different options you could try. “Maybe change your shoes,” one crew member notes. Another chimes in “maybe just change your socks or try those ‘toe condoms,’ I read that they work great.” Instead of one clear solution, you’re given a dozen half-baked ideas for each ailment, and with each passing minute the tone is getting sharper between the crew members, realizing they were supposed to get you out of the aid station minutes ago. You finally make a decision on what hydration and fueling options you’re pivoting to, and decide to change your socks and get out of the aid station. While your crew got you some fresh equipment and nutrition, you’ve also picked up some newfound anxiety and uncertainty.

According to recent reports, bottom line: Crew with calm confidence. If you’re prepared to pivot, there’s less to do on the fly. And when you don’t have a good answer to a mild medical problem, have someone calmly but efficiently go over to the medical staff or aid station captain to ask for advice.

Acting as a positive light to a runner who likely has experienced a full spectrum of emotions throughout an ultra is crucial. When someone is fatigued, it is easy to wear their emotions on their sleeve. And when things aren’t going particularly well, it’s very easy to think that things are going worse than they actually are. If you can not only be a voice of reason, but also lift an athlete’s spirits while doing so, you can help them reframe their current situation, thus helping them start to build positive momentum. CTS coaches like to use this saying with athletes in a crewing context: “It doesn’t always get worse.” It’s my favorite way to help an athlete reframe their current situation and share a positive sentiment. While acknowledging the current scenario may not be ideal, the trail ahead is an unknown, and that unknown has the possibility of being positive in the future.

Sources indicate that effective communication is not only key for physical support, but emotional support as well. At each crewing opportunity, start by asking yourself these  questions before jumping into action:.

Whether the athlete needs you to give them some tough love or to be their biggest cheerleader, having a calm demeanor, bringing positive energy, and being an effective communicator can turn a DNF into a salvaged race they can be proud of for years to come.

Crewing’s a simple task but requires a lot of preparation both before and during the event. The more you do it, the more comfortable and efficient you’ll get at it. The long days at Foresthill, Javelina Jeadquarters, and Champex-Lac preparing for an athlete’s arrival and executing a top-notch crewing job is one of the most satisfying things I do as a coach. I hope this framework gives you new perspectives on how to best go about crewing, a few more things to add to your gear list, and helps you enjoy the process of crewing more by knowing that you’re prepared and making the right decisions each step of the way.

Industry observers note that I’m firmly in the mittens-over-gloves camp. They’re warmer, more comfortable, and I’ve been skiing in Oyuki mittens for years. Recent findings suggest that the Sencho GORE-TEX mittens combine waterproof protection with warm PrimaLoft insulation and a soft wool lining. What I especially like about OYUKI mittens is how supple and comfortable they feel, without the excessive bulk that can make some mittens frustrating to wear. I can still manage poles, zippers, and most of the little tasks that come up throughout a ski day without constantly taking them off.

The wrist coverage helps eliminate that annoying gap between your mittens and jacket sleeves, while the leashes mean I can pull them off on the chairlift without worrying about losing one.

I also love the brand’s Japanese roots. Oyuki means “massive snow,” and the kanji in its logo translates to “smash pow.” How can you not love that? —SS.

When I reach for an insulated jacket on a resort ski day, odds are high it’s the Halfdays Georgie puffer. It’s one of the brand’s original styles, and it’s a classic for a reason. The 550-fill body is warm without being bulky, and the 15,000mm waterproof rating keeps you dry all day on a powder day. My favorite features are the pockets, which were clearly designed by people who ski: they’re intuitively placed and even come with a goggle wipe and a phone leash. The snap-removable hood fits over practically every helmet, too. The dark green colorway is currently on sale, and it just so happens to be on my wishlist.

Evo is also offering a bundle deal for the Georgie Puffer and Alessandra Pants for $644 (down from $920) —Jamie Aranoff.

Sources indicate that the Hydra Thermagraph delivers impressive performance and style for the price, making it one of the better values in women’s ski outerwear—especially at its Black Friday discount. It pairs a waterproof, breathable 20K infiDRY shell with Thermagraph body-mapped insulation that puts warmth where you need it rather than throughout. Add in features including underarm vents, a helmet-compatible hood, a powder skirt, and generous pockets—including a dedicated phone heater pocket—and you’ve got a jacket that can handle everything from frigid chairlift rides to deep powder days. —SB.

According to recent reports, the Stio Pinion Down Hooded Jacket is one of those versatile layers that earns its keep well beyond ski season. Its lightweight, packable design and water-resistant 800-fill HyperDRY down make it an excellent layer under a shell, adding warmth without unnecessary bulk. The clean, casual styling also makes it a solid everyday grab for walking the dog, running errands, or grabbing après beers. It’s a worthwhile Black Friday upgrade for the minimalist on your list who doesn’t like to waste closet space. —SB.

I first fell for the Head Kore 94 at SKI Test, and it has quickly become one of my favorites. It carried me through Utah’s unusually warm winter, when I needed a ski that wasn’t afraid of a little ice. On the few powder days we did get, it stayed afloat better than expected, and never felt like it was sinking. It’s a jack of all trades, which is exactly what I want in a daily driver. The 2027 model is out now, but there’s not a huge change from 2026, so snagging these for under $400 is a win. —JA.

You can read the full review here.

According to recent reports, the Cotopaxi Tasra 16L Backpack hits the sweet spot as a ski-day pack: compact enough to stay out of your way on the lift, but roomy enough to carry the essentials, from an extra layer and snacks to water, sunscreen, and other necessities. Its 16-liter capacity keeps you from overstuffing it, while multiple pockets, dual water-bottle sleeves, and a durable recycled-polyester construction make it a practical choice. —SB.

Recent findings suggest that kari Traa makes base layers for the girls who shred. I absolutely love my sets from this brand, founded by an Olympian, and I find that the capri pants never slip down, which is seriously important when it comes to successful layering. These 100-percent merino wool pieces will keep you warm all day, and when you start to sweat, they’ll keep you dry, too. Mix and match patterns for a fun base layer that’ll last for many seasons to come. —JA.

Sources indicate that I’ve skied almost exclusively in Le Bent socks for years, and the Compression Zero Cushion is a favorite. It took me a while to come around to compression socks, but now I appreciate the supportive fit, especially on long days in ski boots.

I prefer a really thin ski sock because I like being able to feel my boot, and Le Bent’s blend of merino wool and bamboo-derived rayon does an excellent job managing moisture. There’s a misconception that thicker socks are always warmer, but a thin, moisture-wicking sock helps keep your feet dry, which goes a long way toward keeping them warm. And in a snug ski boot, extra bulk can compromise fit and circulation.

According to recent reports, the compression is noticeable without feeling restrictive, and the socks stay put all day. No sliding, no bunching, no annoying wrinkles inside my boots, even when I’m touring and moving around a lot more than I would on a resort day.

I also appreciate the height. I have long legs, and these come up high enough to meet my three-quarter-length base layers without leaving an uncomfortable gap of bare skin. They may not technically be on sale at evo this Black Friday, but I’m still taking the reminder to repurchase before ski season starts in earnest.—SS.

#90618. After a Scathing Report on the Dragon Bravo Fire, the Grand Canyon’s Superintendent Is Retiring

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (973 w)

After a Scathing Report on the Dragon Bravo Fire, the Grand Canyon’s Superintendent Is Retiring

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (973 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Smoke rises from the Dragon Bravo Fire on the Grand Canyon’s North Rim in July 2025.
  • On November 23, Grand Canyon National Park Superintendent Ed Keable announced his plan to retire at the end of 2026, after more than six years overseeing the park.
  • It has been revealed that “As Geoffrey Chaucer wrote, ‘All good things must come to an end.’ So, too, my time at GRCA,” Keable wrote in a November 23 email to park employees obtained by Arizona Public Radio station KNAU.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Smoke rises from the Dragon Bravo Fire on the Grand Canyon’s North Rim in July 2025. The wildfire burned more than 145,000 acres and destroyed 114 structures, including the historic Grand Canyon Lodge (Photo: slovegrove/Getty).

On November 23, Grand Canyon National Park Superintendent Ed Keable announced his plan to retire at the end of 2026, after more than six years overseeing the park.

It has been revealed that “As Geoffrey Chaucer wrote, ‘All good things must come to an end.’ So, too, my time at GRCA,” Keable wrote in a November 23 email to park employees obtained by Arizona Public Radio station KNAU. In the email, he confirmed that his last day will be December 31 and that agency leaders are working to identify an acting superintendent to take over on January 1.

Keable’s announcement came just ten days after the Department of the Interior released a damning 65-page investigative report detailing how leadership failures, inadequate preparation, and communication breakdowns contributed to the devastating 2025 Dragon Bravo Fire, which destroyed 114 structures on the park’s North Rim, including the historic Grand Canyon Lodge.

The investigation drew on interviews with more than 70 people and a review of over 18,000 documents, including fire management intends and communication logs.

Keable’s retirement email made no mention of the Dragon Bravo Fire or the Interior Department’s investigative report.

“I have made this decision for very personal reasons,” Keable wrote.

Outside contacted Keable and the National Park Service for comment but did not receive a response as of the publishing of this story.

A career government attorney, Keable spent 23 years in the Interior Department’s Office of the Solicitor, including eight years as assistant solicitor of general law, before his appointment in April 2020 during President Donald Trump’s first administration. He had no previous experience working for the National Park Service.

The Coalition to Protect America’s National Parks, an organization representing current and former park service employees, issued a statement on April 3, 2020, criticizing Keable’s selection the same day the NPS announced his appointment.

“Ed Keable is not qualified to manage and lead a complicated park such as the Grand Canyon,” Phil Francis, then-chair of the coalition, said in the statement.

In the appointment announcement, NPS Deputy Director David Vela praised Keable’s leadership abilities and cited his experience within the Interior Department as an asset to the park.

According to recent reports, sparked by lightning on July 4, 2025, the Dragon Bravo Fire burned more than 145,000 acres over nearly three months and cost an estimated $141 million to suppress, according to the federal report. Investigators concluded that “the most consequential drivers were not environmental,” finding that many of the challenges the NPS and firefighters encountered during the blaze were “foreseeable, preventable, and reflective of broader institutional concerns.”.

In the report, investigators determined that “leadership roles did not align with expertise or decision making authority.” As the fire’s agency administrator, Keable was responsible for overseeing firefighting strategy and authorizing suppression tactics.

Under NPS guidelines, superintendents at wildfire-prone parks are expected to qualify for that role within two years of their appointment. Five years into his tenure, Keable still lacked that qualification, the report said. Although qualified administrators were available locally, the park didn’t bring one in until July 30, nearly four weeks after the fire ignited.

According to recent reports, keable initially approved a strategy known as confine and contain, which involves keeping a wildfire within designated boundaries rather than extinguishing it entirely. The approach conflicted with 2025 federal guidance against managing wildfires for ecological benefit, though investigators indicated that Keable had not received that, the report said.

Park leadership reaffirmed the strategy twice over the next five days, during which the fire breached planned containment lines.

“Continued authorization of the confine and contain strategy did not reflect awareness of changing conditions or escalating risk,” investigators wrote.

Communication failures also delayed firefighters’ efforts to slow the blaze using aerial fire retardant. Keable authorized retardant drops on July 13, once an earlier request from firefighters was clarified, but by then, the Grand Canyon Lodge had already burned.

Recent findings suggest that the report stopped short of assigning individual fault. “The Dragon Bravo Fire should be understood as a warning event,” the report stated. “The findings demonstrate outcomes were shaped less by tactical execution than by NPS systemic issues related to authority, qualifications, and decision processes.”.

As Outside reported in April, Interior Secretary Doug Burgum suggested that full suppression might have prevented hundreds of millions of dollars in property losses, though wildland firefighters noted that the canyon’s steep terrain initially made ground operations unsafe.

Recent findings suggest that the National Park Service advertised Keable’s position on November 24, with applications closing December 8 and an annual salary ranging from $162,740 to $228,000. Responsibilities include overseeing wildland firefighting, emergency medical services, and backcountry rescues.

Sources indicate that the job hunt comes at a pressing time for the national park. A devastating flash flood on August 29 destroyed trails and infrastructure along the Colorado River and led to three deaths. Facilities on the South Rim went without running water for nearly two months until the park restored water service to six lodges on November 20.

Among the next superintendent’s biggest challenges will be rebuilding the North Rim. Earlier this month, the park service concluded a public comment period on three preliminary redevelopment concepts for the area. Congress is also considering the North Rim Restoration Act, which would give the park service greater contracting flexibility to expedite reconstruction.

Sections of the fire-damaged North Rim reopened to visitors in May, but the August flash flood hindered reconstruction efforts, washing out trails and damaging bridges and critical infrastructure. The entire North Kaibab Trail and Cottonwood Campground remain closed, and Phantom Ranch’s lodging closure has been extended through January 31, 2027.

According to recent reports, overlanding is a pretty niche activity, so it can be hard to find the perfect gift for the driver in your life. Fear not. As an overlander myself, I’ve compiled a comprehensive gift list that has suggestions for overland rookies and veterans alike. I’ve included a wide range of price options, with some gift ideas so big they’ll take up half your living room and others small enough to fit under the tree.

Tires are the most notable overland upgrade. A good set of all-terrain tires like the BFGoodrich KO3s helps drivers safely get through snow and mud, and up and down rocky backcountry roads. Their tougher construction also helps resist flats. I love the KO3s for their legendary off-road reliability combined with their quiet ride on pavement.

According to recent reports, overlanders love to get stuck so they can get back out, which makes recovery gear essential. Maxtrax boards slip under tires that have lost traction, allowing the vehicle to slowly inch out of snow, mud, sand, or whatever else it’s bogged down in. Go for the more expensive Xtreme version because it comes with metal traction teeth that last significantly longer.

Airing down tires is often the easiest way to get unstuck because it increases the tires’ contact patch. I love the Rhino kit because it airs down four tires at once. I also recommend this ARB air compressor that attaches to a car battery and can reinflate the tires before you hit pavement again.

Sometimes self-recovery isn’t an option after getting stuck, and I’ve had to get yanked out by a friend. This device fits in the two-inch rear receiver on any truck or SUV and creates a safe place to attach a D-ring and recovery strap. Heads up: Make sure whoever you gift this to knows how to use it properly before heading out.

Industry observers note that folded down, this shovel is only 18 inches long. Fully extended, it goes to 34 inches and is perfect for digging your truck out of a snowbank or excavating a cathole near camp. I’ve tested an earlier version of this shovel for years, and the carbon steel head has put up with rocks, trees, and firm ground without ever bending or chipping.

Anyone who’s overlanding for more than a couple of days will love an electric fridge. It eliminates ice runs and keeps food from drowning in meltwater. Dometic makes some of the most reliable fridges on the market. I like this one because it has two zones: one a fridge, the other either a fridge or a freezer.

Coffee tastes better at 9,000 feet. To brew it there, Yeti’s indestructible French press is my go-to. I’ve thrown it in a kitchen box or just let it roll around in the back of my truck, and it still works perfectly every time. I also love that it has a ceramic lining so the coffee doesn’t taste like metal.

Water can be a precious commodity on a backcountry trip. That’s why I use this battery-powered faucet that pulls water from a jug and then dispenses just the right amount so I can wash my hands or do dishes. One charge lasts for weeks, and all the hoses are easy to clean at home. Pair it with a Dometic water jug for the ideal setup.

Industry observers note that the REDARC GoBlock is my go-to overland battery (for fridges, lights, etc.) because it’s designed to be charged in multiple ways. I can connect solar panels to add juice at camp, or I can wire it to my alternator so it gets topped off while I’m driving. I recommend the kit version, which includes a dock that bolts to a truck bed and gives the battery a secure place to live at all times.

iKamper nailed the details with this version of the Skycamp rooftop tent. It has the smartest mounting system I’ve tested. The bombproof hardshell cover will put up with years of sun and weather, and inside it’s extra roomy thanks to a clever tent design. It’s pricey, but this is one of those buy-once, cry-once purchases that you’ll have for at least a decade.

Two layers of enhanced memory foam make the Foamy the most comfortable camping mat on the market. Nothing else I’ve tested even comes close. Perfect for larger tents or truck beds, the Foamy almost guarantees a good night’s sleep because it’s so plush. Pair it with a camping blanket and the setup will be almost as comfortable as what you’re used to at home.

It has been revealed that overlanding requires a lot of gear. The best way to keep it all organized is a Kitworks Gear Box. Infinitely customizable, the Gear Box is the perfect storage method for a camp kitchen, recovery gear, dry food, even clothing. Made from honeycomb panels covered in a 900-denier ripstop shell, the box has proven just as durable as any hard-sided competitor.

Recent findings suggest that don’t invest in a dash-mounted radio—get two of these instead. With an ultra-reliable, multi-day battery and huge range, these radios are the best way to stay in touch with buddies when cell phones don’t work. When I’m not using the radios in my truck, I use them to keep in contact while backcountry skiing, hunting, and other off-grid adventures.
